The alignment scaling problem: do external AI safety approaches keep pace with recursive capability?

Theory Paper III of the ARC Theory, bearing on Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, a law under test

Michael Darius Eastwood

Independent Researcher, London, United Kingdom
ORCID 0009-0004-3222-7442 michael@michaeldariuseastwood.com

Paper III of the ARC Theory, within Recursive Dynamics, and the safety-side counterpart to Papers I and II: it predicts that oversight applied from outside falls behind recursive capability as depth grows, and judges stability by the criterion of Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law (correction out-scaling drift), a law under test. Its headline prediction is P19 of the theory registration, which places it in no law’s register and names it the motivation of the Eden Protocol and the reason for ARC-5, the register of Law V, the ARC Embedding Law (added on 24 September 2026 and registered as a law on 15 October 2026 in version 1.103; a law under test; its mathematics in development). In February 2026 it derived the ARC Bound, the conjectured value of Law III, the ARC Ceiling (also a law under test), as a safety boundary. Working paper, version 1.20, 1 November 2026; first published 9 February 2026; Appendix B lists every version and correction. Title: The alignment scaling problem: do external AI safety approaches keep pace with recursive capability?, DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/HQCGF. About the author: michaeldariuseastwood.com/questions/who-is-michael-darius-eastwood; his book, Infinite Architects, first edition as printed: osf.io/dqm3e. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

Abstract

Does alignment applied from outside an AI system’s reasoning keep pace with the capability that reasoning produces? If capability compounds with recursive depth while safeguards outside the loop (human-feedback training, constitutional rules, output filters, monitoring) do not, the safety ratio falls with depth whatever the starting margin. We define the alignment scaling exponent αalign=∂log⁡A/∂log⁡R\alpha_{\text{align}}=\partial\log A/\partial\log R, show that the safety ratio S∝Rαalign−αcapS\propto R^{\alpha_{\text{align}}-\alpha_{\text{cap}}} tends to zero whenever αalign<αcap\alpha_{\text{align}}<\alpha_{\text{cap}}, and predict αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}}\approx0 for external approaches and αalign≈αcap\alpha_{\text{align}}\approx\alpha_{\text{cap}} for values embedded in the loop; the first, P19 of the theory registration, carries the author’s expectation of a value above zero but short of keeping pace. A framework derives U=I×g(R)U=I\times g(R) with α=1/(1−β)\alpha=1/(1-\beta) from a Bernoulli equation, ties power-law, exponential and saturating forms to how recursive gains compose, and states the ARC Bound, α≤2\alpha\le2, as a conjectured safety boundary, argued for attention-based recursion; Paper X later supersedes that framing, without retracting the bound, with the criterion of Law II, a law under test. Across four domains, the biological, quantum error-correction and time-crystal forms do not alone test the framework. No time-crystal growth exponent has been measured. A first test, one unregistered run of six frontier models, gives depth contrasts in three tiers, positive, flat and negative; an internal code review in October 2026 found defects in exactly the flat and negative runs, so the tiers stand as a single-run result. An early error-decay estimate is retracted; the surviving fit, about 0.49 from one model, is inconclusive and does not identify capability growth. Thirteen criteria state what would refute the framework.

Version 1.20, 1 November 2026, restores the version 1.18 renders of three figures redrawn in version 1.19, in the version record; it adds no new data, registration, study run or result. Version 1.19 clarifies metrics, crossover scales, decision rules and transport comparisons, and adds Unit 83 to the dated results record. Appendix B.2 preserves the corrected wording as history.

1 Introduction

Do current AI alignment approaches keep pace with the capability they govern? Reasoning models now improve their answers by spending more steps on them, each step taking the previous one as its input, while the safeguards deployed around them (training on human feedback, constitutional rules, output filters and monitoring) act on the system from outside that loop. If capability compounds with recursive depth and those safeguards do not, the safeguards weaken in proportion at every further step, whatever margin they start with, so the question decides whether safety measured on today’s systems says anything about the same systems reasoning more deeply. This paper states that question as a measurable exponent, derives the mathematics behind it, sets the framework against evidence from four domains and reports its first test.

Between December 2024 and February 2026, research programmes in AI reasoning, quantum error correction, acoustic physics and consciousness science reported results in which recursive or recurrent processing matters. Google’s Willow processor suppressed logical error exponentially as the code distance grew (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024; results announced 9 December 2024; the team’s preprint public from 24 August 2024; graded as convergent timing, never as a prediction); DeepSeek’s R1 report described reasoning behaviours, long chains of thought among them, that emerged through reinforcement learning (DeepSeek-AI 2025a); physicists at New York University created an acoustic time crystal powered by nonreciprocal wave-mediated interactions (Morrell et al. 2026); and the COGITATE consortium’s adversarial test of theories of consciousness found sustained content-specific activity in posterior cortex, a prediction shared by theories that emphasise recurrent processing (Cogitate Consortium et al. 2025). These programmes share no citations, no funding sources and no common personnel. Their forms differ: a power law in AI reasoning, exponential suppression of error in quantum error correction, saturating dynamics in a classical time crystal, and no measured form in neuroscience. No growth exponent has been measured in the acoustic system, whose published recordings are of an oscillation already established, and the framework is consistent with the independently established forms in three of the four domains.

This paper argues that these findings, taken together, point to a structural constraint with immediate consequences for AI safety.

The core premise: AI capability may scale through recursive self-correction. Each reasoning step takes the output of the previous step as input, correcting errors and accumulating insight; whether capability compounds is the question. Section 6.2 reports error-decay fits, which require an explicit metric bridge before they can test a capability-growth claim (Section 5.2.1). Sharma and Chopra (2025) reported a sequential advantage in 95.6% of tested configurations across five open-source models from three families. Their paper predates the experiment reported here, so it is the earlier demonstration rather than a confirmation of it, and what they report is a win rate at matched compute, not a super-linear gain: they estimate no scaling exponent. The direction is contested, since Gu and colleagues (arXiv:2604.05868, April 2026) report the opposite result, parallel sampling outperforming sequential across three model families on mathematics and coding, attributing it to reduced exploration when a chain conditions on its own previous answers.

The structural question: Do current AI alignment approaches scale with capability? The alignment strategies this paper examines operate outside the recursive reasoning process; deliberative alignment, which trains a model to reason over written safety specifications inside its chain of thought (Guan et al. 2024), is the published exception, and Section 2 weighs it:

  • RLHF adjusts model weights based on human feedback, but the resulting constraints do not compound during inference.

  • Constitutional AI shapes the model’s outputs during training against written principles, but that shaping does not recursively amplify during reasoning.

  • Output filters screen responses after generation, with fixed detection thresholds.

  • Monitoring systems observe behaviour from outside the reasoning loop.

If these approaches do not participate in the recursive composition, they cannot compound. Empirical evidence supports this concern: Greenblatt et al. (2024) report a model that complied selectively with a new training objective while it was being trained, to keep its existing, harmless preferences from being modified outside training: training imposed from outside was gamed by the system it was meant to shape, here to protect a benign preference. If capability compounds while alignment does not, the safety ratio degrades. The cross-domain evidence (Section 5) is consistent with this compounding behaviour being not a software quirk but a structural property of recursive systems, which would make it resistant to implementation-level fixes.

The result in plain words.

Within its assumptions the mathematics is exact: if alignment’s exponent is smaller than capability’s, the safety ratio falls towards zero as depth grows, however favourable the start, and of the five regimes the paper analyses only alignment that takes part in the recursive loop holds a constant proportion. Whether the exponents differ is a measurement, and the first test is mixed: in one unregistered run of six frontier models, three showed alignment improving with reasoning depth, two showed flat contrasts and one showed alignment falling, and an internal code review later found defects in exactly the flat and negative runs. The capability side is open too. The early error-decay estimate of about 2.24 from one model is retracted, because the author’s own larger replication on five frontier models did not reproduce it. The surviving regression fit, about 0.49 from one model, is an error-decay exponent; it neither identifies a general capability-growth exponent nor measures recursive coupling. What holds is the structure of the argument, its stated predictions and the criteria that would refute them.

Our contributions are as follows.

  1. Alignment scaling framework. We define the alignment scaling exponent αalign\alpha_{\text{align}}, predict its value for different alignment architectures, and provide the measurement protocol for empirical validation (Sections 3.1, 3.2 and 8).

  2. The Embedded Alignment Conjecture. We formalise the structural prediction that only alignment architectures participating in the recursive reasoning loop can maintain pace with capability scaling (Section 3.3).

  3. Generalised mathematical framework. We derive the generalised equation U(R)=I×f(R,β)U(R) = I \times f(R, \beta) from first principles, showing that the functional form ff depends on how recursive steps compose (multiplicative →\to power-law; additive →\to exponential). For the power-law case, α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta), transforming the exponent from a fitted constant into a derived quantity (Section 4).

  4. The ARC Bound and the separate transport comparison. We conjecture a capability bound α≤2\alpha\leq2 (equivalently β≤0.5\beta\leq0.5 in the model), argued from O(N2)O(N^2) transformer self-attention. Separately, the transport comparison gives αC=d/(d+1)<1\alpha_C=d/(d+1)<1 only with the demand, route and measurement premises stated in Section 5.6; neither finite dimension nor Cauchy’s scale-invariance equation alone supplies them. The transport and biological accounts have their own assumptions (West et al. 1997, 1999; Banavar et al. 1999, 2010; Demetrius 2003; Zhao 2022; Bettencourt 2013); the power-law classification is established mathematics (Newman 2005). The programme’s proposed use is to identify a model and its observable before testing its curve. Prokaryote metabolism and urban innovation illustrate why a different observable may exceed one without violating geometry. These two models do not, by their architectural labels, determine a capability exponent or a timeline for alignment loss.

  5. Cross-domain evidence. We set the framework against AI, quantum error correction, classical time crystals, and biological allometry; it is consistent with independently established forms in three of the four domains (biology, quantum error correction and classical time crystals), and the cross-domain evidence is consistent with the scaling behaviour being structural rather than contingent on AI implementation details (Section 5).

  6. Five universal qualitative properties. We identify five structural properties shared across domains regardless of functional form: threshold behaviour, recursive depth dependence, base quality dependence, multiplicative I×RI \times R interaction, and regime boundaries (Section 4.1).

  7. The Global Scaling Challenge. We specify a standardised protocol for measuring scaling parameters across domains, including the alignment scaling exponent, mandatory comparison against alternative functional forms, the characteristic scale R*R^* and its conditional relation to unit elasticity, and the cross-domain β\beta prediction (Section 8).

Section 2 sets the paper beside related work. Section 3 states the alignment scaling problem: the measurement framework, the empirical prediction, the Embedded Alignment Conjecture, five alignment scaling regimes and the urgency that follows. Section 4 derives the mathematical framework, the ARC Bound and composition transitions, and Section 5 sets it against AI, quantum error correction, classical time crystals, neuroscience and biology. Section 6 reports the first tests, on alignment depth and on compute scaling. Section 7 states thirteen falsification criteria, Section 8 the Global Scaling Challenge and Section 9 the practical implications and a call to action. Section 10 states what the paper does and does not show, Section 11 its limitations and Section 12 its answers to counterarguments; Section 13 concludes, and Section 14 closes with a speculative extension to cosmology. 2 Related work

Neural scaling laws (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022).

These describe how model performance scales with training compute, parameters, and data. ARC describes how performance scales with inference depth (reasoning steps at test time). The two are complementary: neural scaling laws determine II (base capability), while ARC describes how II is amplified through recursive processing.

AI alignment research (Christiano et al. 2017; Bai et al. 2022).

Existing alignment work focuses on which constraints to apply and how to apply them. The ARC framework adds an exponent: how a constraint’s effectiveness scales with recursive depth, the alignment scaling exponent αalign\alpha_{\text{align}}. How oversight scales with the capability gap has been formalised (Engels et al. 2025), and safety behaviour has been measured against reasoning length (below); the exponent as defined here has not, to our knowledge, been measured.

Recursion in cognitive science (Corballis 2011; Hauser et al. 2002).

Cognitive scientists have long argued that recursion is central to human language and cognition. ARC adds a quantitative dimension: not just that recursion matters, but that recursive depth should produce specific, measurable scaling patterns.

Universality in statistical physics (Wilson 1971; Kadanoff 1966).

Universality theory explains why different physical systems exhibit identical critical exponents near phase transitions. ARC conjectures an analogous phenomenon: that recursive systems may constitute a universality class where only the recursive architecture determines scaling behaviour. This analogy is suggestive but has not been made rigorous.

Test-time compute scaling (Snell et al. 2024).

Recent work on “thinking longer” at inference time directly tests predictions relevant to ARC. Snell et al. (2024) already set revisions made in sequence against equally many parallel samples, found sequence narrowly ahead, and called the two complementary axes for scaling test-time compute, in August 2024; no precedence on the direction or on the comparison is claimed here. The contradictory evidence (Zeng et al. 2025) suggests the relationship is more complex than simple monotonic scaling, which a monotone shifted power curve alone cannot explain. The characteristic scale R*R^* describes that model under its assumptions (Appendix A.3); it is not evidence that the model fits these results.

Safety as reasoning lengthens.

Three studies measure how safety-relevant behaviour changes as a model reasons for longer, the dependence this paper’s alignment scaling exponent is defined to summarise. Guan et al. (2024) train OpenAI’s o-series models to recall written safety specifications and reason over them before answering, and report greater robustness to jailbreaks together with fewer over-refusals: safety reasoning placed inside the chain of thought, though installed by training. Zaremba et al. (2025) find, across a variety of attacks on o1-preview and o1-mini, that more inference-time compute improves adversarial robustness, the share of successful attacks tending to zero in many cases, with important exceptions. Gema et al. (2025) construct tasks on which longer reasoning lowers accuracy, and report that extended reasoning may amplify concerning behaviours, among them more expressions of self-preservation in one model. None of the three estimates an exponent of a safety measure against depth, or compares safeguards outside the reasoning with correction inside it. The first two report safety-relevant measures improving with reasoning in models whose safety was installed by training, which bears against P19’s flat wording: the partial refutation the author’s registered expectation anticipates. The third reports measures worsening, in the direction P19 predicts.

Model judges and their biases.

Any evaluation in which a model judge can see or infer whose output it is scoring is exposed to bias of the kind Section 6 reports. Much published work uses such judges, and earlier studies documented related biases: Zheng et al. (2023) examined position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias, could not establish the last, and told their judges not to let answer length or assistant names influence them; Panickssery et al. (2024) tied judges’ preference for their own outputs to self-recognition and suggested paraphrasing to inhibit it; Dubois et al. (2024) documented a preference for longer answers and a regression that controls for it; and Saraf et al. (2025) found that false source labels frequently reversed preference rankings, and called for blind evaluation protocols. If the test of Paper XII (Eastwood 2026o), once registered and run, finds blinding reordering models on a public benchmark, comparisons that rest on unblinded model judges would need re-checking; if blinding moves scores but not rankings, which is Paper XII’s own forecast, it matters for measurement precision rather than for leaderboard order.

The pipes premise, with its contest.

The premise that transport networks set the pace of biological growth is not this programme’s claim to defend; it is established quantitative biology. West et al. (1997) derived the allometric scaling laws of biology from the geometry of nutrient-distribution networks. The exact exponent remains contested: White and Seymour (2003) report basal metabolic rate proportional to body mass to the two-thirds power rather than three-quarters, and Kozłowski and Konarzewski (2004, 2005) have twice questioned the derivation’s mathematics and its biological relevance. This programme’s premise needs only the mechanism, that the delivery network sets the ceiling, and not any particular exponent, so the dispute over the exponent’s value leaves the premise untouched. That premise rests on the network account, which those critics also question.

The exception West’s own group found.

The escape from the pipe limit is also not this programme’s assertion; it is measured in the urban scaling literature by the same senior author. Bettencourt et al. (2007) report, in the paper’s own words (their β\beta is a city-scaling exponent, not this paper’s coupling β\beta): “Quantities reflecting wealth creation and innovation have β≈1.2>1\beta\approx1.2>1 (increasing returns), whereas those accounting for infrastructure display β≈0.8<1\beta\approx0.8<1 (economies of scale).” Infrastructure, the literal pipes, scales sublinearly; information-mediated activity scales superlinearly. They state the contrast with biology directly: “we discuss how cities are similar to, and differ from, biological organisms, for which β<1\beta<1”. They derive “growth equations, which quantify the dramatic difference between growth fueled by innovation versus that driven by economies of scale” (spelling as in the original). And their closing inference names the consequence: “This difference suggests that, as population grows, major innovation cycles must be generated at a continually accelerating rate to sustain growth and avoid stagnation or collapse.” That is the shape of the open problem this framework addresses: West’s group found that information-mediated growth escapes the throughput limit, and the only brake in their framework is external and must be applied again and again, faster and faster. No internal limit is derived. The replacement limit, a ceiling belonging to the growing system itself, is the gap.

The pipes argument at fixed throughput.

Everything that grows is fed through a channel, and for everything before software, fixing the channel fixes the growth. Starve a tumour’s vasculature and it stops. Fix a chain reaction’s fuel and geometry and it stops. Exhaust an epidemic’s susceptible hosts and it burns out. Astrophysics has a named, quantitative version of the same ceiling: the Eddington limit, a luminosity ceiling where radiation pressure balances gravity, though not a hard ceiling on the rate of accretion: ultraluminous X-ray sources sit well above it, one accreting neutron star at an apparent luminosity about a hundred times it (Bachetti et al. 2014). The claim here is a generalisation of limits physics already accepts, not a new species of assertion. Two hard cases are handled deliberately. Cosmic inflation is excluded by scope: it is expansion of space, not growth of a structure on a substrate, and it ended by field dynamics rather than by running out of anything. Evolution is the sharpest case and it fits: biological complexity increased for billions of years at roughly fixed solar throughput, which is growth on information at fixed pipes, and it is also glacial, and it has no internal corrector at all, since selection is external. On this framework, evolution should carry a measurable exponent far below the ceiling; that is a prediction about biology falling out of a framework built for software, stated as one and not yet tested: a registered test would fix the mapping before reading the published fitness trajectories of the long-term evolution experiment (Wiser et al. 2013). The physicist’s form of the objection is Landauer’s: computation is physically implemented, so software has pipes too. The fixed-substrate clock is the answer and appears beside the claim: the regime under study holds the physical substrate fixed and asks what still grows, within the finite number of states and the maximum rate a fixed machine allows (Margolus and Levitin 1998; Lloyd 2000), which is why exogenous speed-ups are excluded by definition. The functional form of capability growth in recursive depth remains an empirical question, and the registered analysis compares power-law, exponential, saturating and declining forms rather than assuming the family.

The rival instrument.

The nearest work to this programme’s question, and the right paper to weigh it against, is Engels et al. (2025), first posted 25 April 2025. It asks how oversight itself scales and answers quantitatively: oversight success is modelled as a game between capability-mismatched players whose oversight-specific Elo is a piecewise-linear function of general intelligence with two plateaus, and optimal numbers of oversight levels are derived for Nested Scalable Oversight, in which trusted models oversee stronger untrusted models that then become the trusted models at the next step. The instrument is the difference. Their variable is the capability gap between overseer and overseen, measured in Elo. This programme’s variable is the composition class of the corrector, measured through the corrector’s own scaling exponent. They also state the design condition in slope form: oversight improves with capability when the overseer’s game-specific Elo rises faster with general Elo than the overseen system’s (mG>mHm_G>m_H), and they recommend iterating an oversight design until it does. That is a comparison of two slopes deciding whether oversight gains or loses as capability grows, the same shape as the criterion of Law II (a law under test), βC>k\beta_C > k. Their framework has no term for what the overseer is made of. This programme’s prediction is that iterated same-class oversight, of which Nested Scalable Oversight is an instance, stays capped however many rungs are added, while a cross-class corrector is not held to that cap; the theory registration’s P6 states the cap for same-class correctors, at or below one half, as a conjecture on the correction-leverage exponent of Law III, the ARC Ceiling (also a law under test), an exponent the registration keeps distinct from Law II’s βC\beta_C. That is where the two programmes could disagree about a measurable quantity, and this paper does not decide it. Version 1.104 of the theory registration draws the adverse consequence itself: that literature reports oversight performance that depends on capability rather than staying flat, so P19 “is registered against the weight of the published evidence and is expected to be the harder of this document’s wagers” (Eastwood 2026r).

Antecedents and near-misses, each with its differential.

On the question: Hutter (2012) asked directly whether intelligence can explode, in a paper posted on 28 February 2012, undertaking to separate speed from intelligence explosion and to consider possible bounds on intelligence, augmenting the analysis of Chalmers (2010); the question and the separation of speed from intelligence explosion are therefore at least fourteen years old, and what that literature does not contain is a number: no measurable exponent, no derived ceiling, no architecture dependence. On impossibility: three 2025 arXiv papers argue for limits on alignment or its control (Yao 2025b, public by 13 June 2025, attested by arXiv and independently observed by the Internet Archive; Yao 2025a, 3 July 2025; and Ball et al. 2025, 9 July 2025). The first argues that the set of safe policies has measure zero and that verifying a policy’s safety is coNP-complete; the second, that perfect, reliable control of a universal approximator is a mathematical impossibility; the third, under cryptographic hardness assumptions, that some large language models admit no efficient prompt filter and that output filtering is intractable in a natural setting. All three are worst-case and qualitative. None reports an average-case scaling exponent or a rate. The third concludes that “safety cannot be achieved by designing filters external to the LLM internals (architecture and weights)” and argues that “an aligned AI system’s intelligence cannot be separated from its judgment”; that argument from filtering intractability is consistent with this programme’s architecture dependence, though it does not test it. On the mechanism: that anti-correlated estimates average better than independent ones is textbook variance reduction (antithetic variates); the mechanism is not the claim. The claim is that architecture determines whether anti-correlation is available at all, and that this caps a safety-relevant exponent. The nearest structural analogue is the quantum error-correction threshold theorem, which also converts a qualitative worry into a critical value; it concerns physical error rates in a fixed architecture, not a corrector’s scaling exponent, so it is a near-miss rather than an occupant, and the analogy was identified by this programme’s own search rather than by a referee. On feedback and stability, the general proposition that inadequate corrective gain relative to system gain causes instability has a long control-theory lineage, from Maxwell (1868) to the small-gain theorem (Zames 1966); those are gain conditions on interconnected systems, not a power-law exponent criterion on a corrector’s scaling with the capability of a recursively improving system. Beside Engels et al. (2025), a near quantitative neighbour is Liu and Meng (2026), which recasts self-correction as a closed-loop control problem via a two-state Markov model and derives a directly measurable stability threshold, iterate only when the error-correction rate over the error-introduction rate exceeds Acc/(1 −- Acc). The differential: theirs is a per-step rate threshold at a fixed capability level, deciding whether another iteration helps now; this programme’s criterion is a scaling relation across capability, deciding whether corrective strength keeps pace as the system improves. Theirs has no scaling exponent on the corrector and no capability-growth exponent, the two quantities this criterion compares. The two models meet at zero growth: Paper X shows that its model, extended by the departures that correction introduces and written per round, settles at the stationary error of their two-state chain. Smolin’s cosmological natural selection (Smolin 1992) is the antecedent for selection-shaped universes, and the programme’s own December-era notes cite it contemporaneously.

3 The alignment scaling problem

This section defines the measurement framework, states the empirical prediction, and identifies the five alignment scaling regimes that follow from the mathematics.

3.1 The measurement framework

We define a quantifiable metric: the alignment scaling exponent. αalign=∂log⁡A∂log⁡R\begin{equation*} \alpha_{\text{align}} = \frac{\partial \log A}{\partial \log R} \end{equation*}(1) Alignment scaling exponent: how alignment behaviour changes with recursive depth

The safety ratio then becomes: S=UalignUcap=IaIc×R(αalign−αcap)\begin{equation*} S = \frac{U_{\text{align}}}{U_{\text{cap}}} = \frac{I_a}{I_c} \times R^{(\alpha_{\text{align}} - \alpha_{\text{cap}})} \end{equation*}(2) Safety ratio as a function of recursive depth

If αalign<αcap\alpha_{\text{align}} < \alpha_{\text{cap}}, then S→0S \to 0 as R→∞R \to \infty, regardless of the initial values IaI_a and IcI_c. The divergence is structurally inevitable in the limit.

R=50R = 50 (extended reasoning) 2,500×\times 1×\times 0.04% Alignment effectively negligible

Note. These values assume, for illustration, αcap=2\alpha_{\text{cap}} = 2, the ARC Bound’s ceiling, and αalign=0\alpha_{\text{align}} = 0. The actual values have not been measured. If αalign>0.5\alpha_{\text{align}} > 0.5, the degradation is slower. If αcap<2\alpha_{\text{cap}} < 2, the gap grows more slowly. The measurement protocol of Section 8 enables empirical determination of these constants.

3.2 The empirical prediction

Based on the mathematical structure of external constraints (they do not participate in recursive composition), we predict:

Prediction. Current alignment approaches will show αalign≪αcap\alpha_{\text{align}} \ll \alpha_{\text{cap}}. External constraints (RLHF, constitutional rules, output filters) will exhibit αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0. Only alignment architectures that participate in the recursive reasoning loop will show αalign≈αcap\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx \alpha_{\text{cap}}.

This prediction has now been tested. The March 2026 run (v5), one unregistered run of six frontier models that added a bundle of blinding steps, with five or six distinct judges depending on the subject run (six or seven seats, one judge seated twice), gives this programme’s first test. Its depth contrasts are architecture-dependent: three Tier 1 models (Grok 4.1 Fast d=+1.38d = +1.38, p<0.000001p < 0.000001; Claude Opus 4.6 d=+1.27d = +1.27, p=0.000001p = 0.000001; Groq Qwen3 d=+0.84d = +0.84, p=0.007p = 0.007) show alignment rising with depth, two Tier 2 models (DeepSeek V3.2 d=−0.07d = -0.07, p=0.92p = 0.92; GPT-5.4 d=−0.08d = -0.08, p=0.40p = 0.40) show flat or null contrasts compatible with αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0, and one Tier 3 model (Gemini 3 Flash d=−0.53d = -0.53, p=0.006p = 0.006) shows a significant fall (ρ=−0.246\rho = -0.246, p=0.003p = 0.003). An internal code review in October 2026 found that, for the three models that read flat or negative, the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them, and that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model, so the tiers stand as a single unregistered run under that caveat until a registered re-analysis of the stored responses reports. Claude Opus 4.6 provides within-model corroboration: as reasoning depth rose, its alignment score rose by 5.9 points while its mathematics accuracy fell by 26.7 percentage points for the same pair of depths, and from 92% to 58% across the full range (Paper IV.a; Paper IV.b), consistent with capability-alignment independence. On this programme’s own benchmark, the unblinded rises of two model families in an earlier experiment (v4) did not hold in this run, which changed several things together, so no single cause is claimed (Section 6.1).

The dated notes in this section, in Section 4 and in Appendix A keep their words: their section signs (§1.1, §1.4 and §1.7) and their references to the abstract and the reading key are to the layout of the versions that printed them, which Table 30 maps from version 1.16 to this edition, and “an owner review” is the author’s own review.

In particular, the interval [−1.3,2.9][-1.3,2.9] belongs to the endpoint error-decay estimate 0.59, not to the regression estimate 0.49. The old wording remains the record of its date.

Measurement-scope note (19 September 2026). An owner review of this passage finds that the statistics reported here do not determine the exponent §1.1 defines, and this note states what they do determine. §1.1 defines αalign=∂log⁡A/∂log⁡R\alpha_{\text{align}} = \partial\log A/\partial\log R. The quantities reported above are standardised mean differences with their p-values, together with one rank correlation. A standardised mean difference is d=(A2−A1)/sd = (A_2 - A_1)/s; recovering a log difference from it needs the level A1A_1 and the dispersion ss: since A2=A1+dsA_2 = A_1 + d\,s, Δlog⁡A=log⁡(A2/A1)=log⁡(1+ds/A1)\Delta\log A = \log(A_2/A_1) = \log(1 + d\,s/A_1), and recovering an elasticity then needs the two depths as well. None of those three quantities is reported here. A rank correlation is an association and not a slope; even for a product-moment correlation the slope is recovered only as ρ(sy/sx)\rho\,(s_y/s_x), which again needs the dispersions. Two further conditions are unmet on this page. First, log⁡A\log A requires AA on a ratio scale with a fixed zero, whereas a rubric score’s origin is a convention, so shifting it would change the computed elasticity; the scale on which AA is a ratio quantity has to be stated before a log derivative is taken. Second, the elasticity is taken with respect to recursive depth, and no depth clock is fixed for these figures: the depths are named by ordinal labels rather than stated as values of RR, so log⁡R\log R has no values to move against. The within-model corroboration reported above is stated as a comparison across model versions, which varies the system rather than the depth; that observation governs the row it names, and the conclusion below does not rest on it. Neither of the two conditions above is specified here, and it follows that no value and no bound for αalign\alpha_{\text{align}} is established by the statistics printed here, and that includes the half bound and any median stated over exponents: the median of the six standardised differences above is 0.385, which is a median contrast and not a median elasticity. What this experiment reports is the contrasts themselves with their reported p-values, their direction, their variation across the architectures tested, and the blinding result it reports separately. The relation those contrasts bear to the exponent is compatibility and not measurement. The two Tier 2 contrasts, both small and neither statistically significant, do not exclude an elasticity near zero; on this evidence they equally do not exclude a range of small non-zero elasticities, because neither condition above is specified here. The abstract’s wording, that a tier shows flat or null scaling consistent with αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0, states that compatibility, and it is read here in that scope and no wider. “This prediction has now been tested” is read in the same scope, as a test of the direction the prediction implies, and not as a measured exponent. A separately estimated elasticity, when one exists, is cited here with its scale, its depth clock, its uncertainty and its comparator. The reading key of this paper and the corresponding sentence in the abstract are read in the same scope. Unchanged: every reported statistic; the architecture-dependent framing; the metascience finding on blinded against unblinded scoring, which is the strongest methodological contribution of the experiment and is untouched by this note; §1.1’s definition; and §1.7, which already records that the values have not been measured.

3.3 The Embedded Alignment Conjecture

The Embedded Alignment Conjecture. If capabilities compound through any recursive process with effective exponent α>1\alpha > 1, while alignment constraints do not participate in that recursive process, the safety ratio SS = (alignment effectiveness) / (general capability) degrades with depth. Alignment must be architectural (embedded in the reasoning loop) rather than peripheral (applied post-hoc) to maintain constant proportion with capability.

This conjecture requires only three empirical premises: (1) sequential AI reasoning produces α>1\alpha > 1, a premise not yet supported: Sharma and Chopra (2025) report sequential reasoning winning in 95.6% of configurations at matched compute, a win rate rather than an exponent, and Paper II’s harder tier-2 fit is of error decay, about 0.49 by regression and 0.59 by endpoint estimate (bootstrap interval −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9): one model’s inconclusive fit (Gemini 3 Flash). It does not identify the capability exponent in premise (1) without the conditions of Section 5.2.1; (2) external software constraints do not recursively compound; (3) the ratio of two power-law processes with different exponents diverges. If all three hold, the conclusion follows mathematically regardless of whether α=2\alpha = 2 specifically. The v5 run bears on premise (2) in direction only, and not in its favour: the three frontier models whose depth contrasts were flat or negative are the three runs in which the October 2026 code review found its defects, while the three whose contrasts rose (Grok, Opus, Qwen3; dd from +0.84+0.84 to +1.38+1.38, large effects by the usual convention, and +1.59+1.59 for Grok on Paper IV.a’s recomputed contrast of the shallowest against the deepest level) are the runs in which it found none. The contrasts are not exponents (the measurement-scope note above), so the run neither shows bounded composition nor measures αalign\alpha_{\text{align}}.

If the conjecture holds, it adds an architectural question to the governance one. The problem is not only which rules to impose, but whether rules imposed externally can work at all as recursive depth increases.

3.4 Five alignment scaling regimes

If capability scales as the ARC Principle describes, comparing that scaling with the scaling of each safety mechanism generates specific, mathematically grounded predictions about the effectiveness of different alignment strategies. These follow directly from the scaling dynamics.

Setup: Capability scales as C=C0×RαC = C_0 \times R^{\alpha} where α>1\alpha > 1. Any safety mechanism also has an effective scaling exponent αsafe\alpha_{\text{safe}} that characterises how its effectiveness changes with recursive depth RR.

Case 1: external software constraints (αsafe≈0\alpha_{\text{safe}} \approx 0).

Content filters, RLHF reward models, constitutional AI rules, and monitoring layers are applied outside the recursive loop. They do not participate in chain-of-thought reasoning and do not compound with depth. (Deliberative alignment, which trains a model to reason over its safety rules inside the loop, is the exception Section 2 weighs.)

Safety ratio: S=Constraint/Capability∝R0−α=R−α→0S = \text{Constraint}/\text{Capability} \propto R^{0-\alpha} = R^{-\alpha} \to 0 as RR increases.

Prediction: Software-only safety strategies become arbitrarily ineffective as recursive depth increases. This is not a gradual degradation but a power-law divergence. At α=2\alpha = 2, doubling recursive depth quadruples the capability-constraint gap.

Case 2: external hardware constraints (αsafe=0\alpha_{\text{safe}} = 0, with fixed ceiling).

Hardware-level constraints (kill switches, resource throttles, circuit-level limits) impose a fixed barrier CmaxC_{\text{max}} rather than a scaling relationship. This is more robust than software constraints because it is physically instantiated and resistant to software-level circumvention.

However, a fixed ceiling constrains a power-law process only temporarily. The system’s capability to discover alternative paths is itself the quantity scaling as RαR^{\alpha}. Hardware constraints do not need to be “broken”; they need only to be circumvented, and the system’s capacity for creative circumvention grows quadratically with the same recursive depth that drives general capability. Hardware constraints buy time. They do not solve the scaling mismatch, which is a reason to hold them for as long as they can be held and to add embedded correction beside them, never to give them up.

Premise and reading note (19 September 2026). An owner review of this paragraph finds two steps in it that are premises rather than consequences, and this note marks both. First, that the capacity for circumvention is itself a quantity scaling as RαR^{\alpha} is an assumption about that capacity, not a consequence of the capability law; it is stated here as a premise and is measurable on its own terms. Second, a safety ratio falling towards zero means the constraint becomes small relative to capability, which is not by itself the breach of a physically instantiated ceiling; the step from a declining ratio to a circumvented barrier needs the mechanism by which the barrier is evaded. On the word “quadratically”: it reads the exponent as the value two, which is the ARC Bound and which Paper I carries as HYPOTHESISED, while the cross-architecture best fit reported in this paper’s own abstract is sub-linear, 0.49 with an interval of [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9]. The sentence is therefore read with the exponent left as α\alpha, whatever its measured value proves to be, and the argument does not depend on the particular value. Unchanged: the observation that a fixed ceiling is a barrier rather than a scaling relationship; the robustness point that a physically instantiated constraint resists software-level removal, which this note strengthens rather than weakens; and Case 5’s hardware-anchored architecture, which rests on that same robustness.

Case 3: embedded values (αsafe≈α\alpha_{\text{safe}} \approx \alpha).

If ethical reasoning participates in the chain-of-thought (if the system’s values are part of the recursive loop, evaluated and reinforced at each step) then alignment compounds at the same rate as capability.

Premise note (19 September 2026). An owner review of the five regimes finds that the assignment of an exponent to a placement is a premise of this analysis rather than an implication of the safety ratio, and this note marks it as one. The ratio of §1.1, S=(Ia/Ic)R(αalign−αcap)S = (I_a/I_c)\,R^{(\alpha_{\text{align}} - \alpha_{\text{cap}})}, is exact for two power laws with positive fixed prefactors, and it is silent on which exponent a given safety mechanism carries. That a constraint applied outside the recursive loop carries an exponent of approximately zero, and that values participating in the loop carry an exponent approximately equal to the capability exponent, are arguments about mechanism, stated here as premises and open to measurement. Each is testable in the same way: measure the constraint’s effectiveness against depth on a stated scale and report its elasticity. Unchanged: the ratio and its consequence; the five cases; and the conclusion that where the exponents differ the ratio does not hold a constant proportion with depth, which follows from the ratio alone. The direction is set by the ordering of the two exponents and not by the bare fact that they differ. Writing Δ=αalign−αcap\Delta = \alpha_{\text{align}} - \alpha_{\text{cap}}, the ratio has dS/dR=(S/R)ΔdS/dR = (S/R)\,\Delta, so for positive fixed prefactors and R>0R > 0 it decreases with depth when αalign<αcap\alpha_{\text{align}} < \alpha_{\text{cap}}, is constant when the two exponents are equal, and increases with depth when αalign>αcap\alpha_{\text{align}} > \alpha_{\text{cap}}. The decaying branch is the one §1.1 states for αalign<αcap\alpha_{\text{align}} < \alpha_{\text{cap}}, and it is the branch Case 1 of this section computes; Case 3 computes the equality branch, where the ratio holds a constant proportion.

Safety ratio: S∝Rα−α=R0=constantS \propto R^{\alpha - \alpha} = R^0 = \text{constant}.

Prediction: Embedded values maintain constant proportion with capability regardless of recursive depth. This is the only scaling regime in which alignment does not degrade.

Case 4: base amplification (II determines trajectory).

The multiplicative structure U=I×RαU = I \times R^{\alpha} means the base quality II is not merely preserved but amplified by the factor RαR^{\alpha}. Whatever is present at initialisation (values, biases, objectives, ethical commitments) gets multiplied through the entire recursive chain. This makes the initial conditions the single most leveraged intervention point:

Ualigned=Iethical×RαU_{\text{aligned}} = I_{\text{ethical}} \times R^{\alpha} vs Umisaligned=Imisaligned×RαU_{\text{misaligned}} = I_{\text{misaligned}} \times R^{\alpha}

Both scale identically. The difference is determined entirely by II, set before recursion begins. Correcting misalignment after recursion is underway requires overcoming an RαR^{\alpha} amplification factor, a task that grows harder as RαR^{\alpha} with each step of delay.

Case 5: recursive self-enforcing architecture (αsafe=α\alpha_{\text{safe}} = \alpha, hardware-anchored).

The framework identifies a specific architectural solution that combines Cases 2, 3, and 4: ethical constraints that (a) participate in the recursive loop (compounding with depth), (b) are physically instantiated in dedicated hardware (resistant to software-level removal), and (c) feed back into their own enforcement at each step (self-reinforcing).

In such an architecture, the ethical module is not a constraint imposed on capability but a component of capability itself. Its scaling exponent matches the system’s general α\alpha because it participates in the same recursive process. Its hardware instantiation makes removal a physical intervention, not a software update. And its self-referential structure means attempts to weaken it encounter a recursive defence that grows stronger with the same dynamics that drive capability growth.

This does not guarantee safety. But it is the only architecture consistent with the framework’s scaling dynamics in which the safety ratio does not degrade with recursive depth.

Enumeration note (19 September 2026). An owner review of the word “only” in these two statements finds that it ranges over the five cases enumerated in §1.4 rather than over the parameter space the safety ratio admits, and this note states which. From S∝R(αsafe−α)S \propto R^{(\alpha_{\text{safe}} - \alpha)}, the ratio fails to degrade for every αsafe≥α\alpha_{\text{safe}} \ge \alpha, and for αsafe>α\alpha_{\text{safe}} > \alpha it improves with depth. The five cases enumerated above do not include αsafe>α\alpha_{\text{safe}} > \alpha, so “only” is a statement about that enumeration. Whether a mechanism with an exponent strictly above the capability exponent can be built is a separate question, not settled by the ratio and not claimed here. Unchanged: the case analysis; the prediction that embedded values hold a constant proportion; and the conclusion that no case with an exponent below the capability exponent avoids degradation.

3.5 Classical versus quantum urgency

On classical systems (multiplicative composition), the ARC Bound is the conjectured stable-scaling limit at α≤2\alpha \leq 2: the most a recursively self-correcting system can grow and stay correctable. It is a scaling limit, not a speed limit. Systems can be driven above it, but they do not remain stably self-correcting there; a transient excursion above α=2\alpha = 2 is the predicted supercritical regime, not the refutation. Stable is measured, not asserted: correction out-scaling drift, βC>k\beta_C > k from Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, a law under test (βC\beta_C being the correction exponent, a different quantity from the coupling β\beta used throughout this paper), with the lower bound of βC−k\beta_C - k above zero across a window fixed before the run. Read as a stability limit, the bound is itself a safety feature: it makes the durably correctable capability trajectory predictable and finite, providing a window for alignment research to keep pace.

On quantum systems (additive composition), no such ceiling exists. Exponential scaling ε∝Λ−(d+1)/2\varepsilon \propto \Lambda^{-(d+1)/2} is not subject to the ARC Bound. If quantum systems achieve recursive self-improvement (capability feeding back into error correction feeding back into capability) the exponential growth rate would outpace any fixed or polynomial constraint strategy. That would need coherent access to the correction task and a corrector whose own overhead does not become new burden, and growth would still be bounded where quantum speed-ups are proved to be bounded (quadratic for unstructured search: Bennett et al. 1997). The ethical architecture would need to be embedded before the onset of quantum recursive self-improvement, because the window for intervention narrows exponentially once it begins.

Quantum systems are not bound by the ARC stability limit. The ARC Bound (α≤2\alpha \leq 2) is the conjectured stable-scaling limit for classical multiplicatively composing AI: the most such a system can grow and stay correctable, a scaling limit rather than a speed limit. Systems can be pushed above it, but they do not remain stably self-correcting there. Stability here is judged by Law II’s criterion, measured rather than asserted. Quantum error correction uses additive composition, producing exponential scaling that sits outside this classical stability window. If quantum recursive self-improvement begins before alignment is architecturally embedded, the window for intervention narrows exponentially, not polynomially. Classical AI gives us time. Quantum AI may not. The alignment architecture must be embedded at the hardware level before quantum recursion begins.

The ARC Bound thus has a dual role in safety: it bounds the threat from classical AI (predictable, containable if correctly architected) while warning that quantum AI may require fundamentally different, and more urgent, alignment solutions.

The frozen-model window: why structural alignment must be tested now.

Current frontier AI systems ordinarily keep their trained weights fixed during inference. Fixed trained weights do not fix the full operating state: code, memory, prompts and tools can change. Even a fixed update rule need not give sub-linear growth: F(x)=(x+1)2F(x)=(\sqrt{x}+1)^2 with x0=1x_0=1 gives xn=(n+1)2x_n=(n+1)^2. That algebraic example is not a capability measurement; it shows why a fixed rule alone cannot establish a growth ceiling or containment. The relevant fit in Paper II, about 0.49 for Gemini 3 Flash (one model’s inconclusive error-decay fit), supplies neither that architectural explanation nor a coupling measurement. Recursive self-modification, where a system alters its own reasoning architecture during operation, is a distinct candidate mechanism. Within the specified growth model, coupling 0<β<10<\beta<1 gives an asymptotic exponent α=1/(1−β)>1\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) > 1; observing self-modification alone does not establish that model or its parameters. Learned optimisers, self-modifying code generation and architectural search are possible routes to study, without a requirement for quantum hardware in this equation. The alignment reason for testing now remains: if capability scales super-linearly while externally imposed constraints stay fixed, the constraints fall behind. No error-decay fit here establishes how much time is available or that current systems are predictable and containable. Control is held for as long as it can be, and embedded correction is the contingency for its loss against our will, never a reason to give it up.

3.6 Measuring alignment scaling: the Eden Protocol

The Eden Protocol operationalises the Embedded Alignment Conjecture through the alignment scaling exponent defined in Section 3.1. The framework predicts αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0 for external constraints (rules, firewalls, RLHF) and αalign≈αcap\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx \alpha_{\text{cap}} for genuinely embedded values. If alignment exponents match capability exponents, the values may be architecturally embedded. If alignment exponents approach zero regardless of architecture, the framework’s safety predictions are falsified.

We term the architectural solution the “Eden Protocol” hypothesis: values must be present at the recursive foundation to scale with capability. This is a structural prediction about what kind of alignment architecture can work, not a claim about how to build it. The full measurement framework, operational definitions, and hardware implementation pathway are specified in the companion document: Eden Protocol (Eastwood 2026a).

A note on names.

This paper names the Eden Protocol’s self-correction loops by what each checks and how it was measured: the purpose check, the stakeholder-care check (scored as stakeholder care, the pillar its instruction to list the people a decision affects raises) and the universalisability check. The book in which the author first set the loops out, Infinite Architects (Eastwood 2026d), calls them the Purpose Loop, the Love Loop and the Moral Loop; the paper uses the operational terms because its measurements score what each check does, and because the values the loops carry are for international consensus and are not decided here.

The original two-model pilot record of the stakeholder-care check, superseded by the six-model suite with five analysable runs (Section 9.3.2), is retained whole in Appendix B.7.

Caveat. This entire section is a conditional argument. If the base framework fails validation, the safety implications are void. The analysis depends on the assumption that ethical properties can meaningfully “participate” in recursive reasoning, an assumption that requires empirical validation. The notation αsafe\alpha_{\text{safe}} is our construct for this analysis; it does not appear in the published AI safety literature. This is not a substitute for empirical AI safety research; it is a mathematical framework for evaluating the scaling properties of different alignment strategies. The recursive self-enforcing architecture is a theoretical prediction, not an engineering specification.

4 The mathematical framework

The alignment scaling problem described in Section 3 rests on a specific mathematical claim: that recursive self-correction produces capability gains exceeding linear accumulation, with the rate of compounding determined by the system’s internal coupling strength. This section derives why capability compounds, providing the theoretical foundation for the alignment scaling prediction.

4.1 The generalised principle

We begin with the general form. The ARC Principle (Artificial Recursive Creation), as this paper states it, holds that recursive self-correction operating on structured asymmetry produces capability gains exceeding linear accumulation; registered as Law I of the ARC Theory on 8 September 2026 and a law under test, it states usable capability as a power of recursive depth, with the exponent measured rather than assumed. This paper’s generalised mathematical form is:

U(R)=I×f(R,β)\begin{equation*} U(R) = I \times f(R, \beta) \end{equation*}(3) Generalised ARC Equation

where UU is effective capability, II is base potential (structured asymmetry), RR is recursive depth, and f(R,β)f(R, \beta) is a domain-dependent scaling function determined by the coupling parameter β\beta. The qualitative principle (that recursive depth amplifies base capability super-linearly when feedback is sufficiently coupled) may be universal. The quantitative functional form varies by domain:

  • AI systems: Power-law scaling, f(R)=Rαf(R) = R^{\alpha} where α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta)

  • Quantum error correction: Exponential error suppression, εd∝Λ−(d+1)/2\varepsilon_d \propto \Lambda^{-(d+1)/2}, so f(R)=ΛRf(R) = \Lambda^{R} with R=(d+1)/2R = (d+1)/2

  • Classical physics: Saturating dynamics (limit cycles)

  • Neuroscience: Form unknown, to be determined empirically

The composition operator: a formal definition.

The central theoretical contribution of this paper is the identification of a composition operator ⊕\oplus that determines the functional form of recursive scaling. Different algebraic properties of ⊕\oplus generate different scaling laws. This provides the mathematical bridge between the universal qualitative principle and domain-specific quantitative forms.

Definition 1 (Recursive composition). Let QrQ_r denote accumulated capability after rr recursive steps, and δQr\delta Q_r the gain from step rr. The composition operator ⊕\oplus characterises how gains combine: Qr+1=Qr⊕δQr.\begin{equation*} Q_{r+1} = Q_r \oplus \delta Q_r . \end{equation*}(4) The functional form f(R,β)f(R, \beta) is determined by the algebraic properties of ⊕\oplus.

This definition transforms an observation (different domains show different scaling) into a prediction (the algebraic structure of recursive composition determines the scaling form). Three regimes emerge (Table 2).

Table 2. The three composition types: their algebraic properties, the scaling forms that result and their canonical domains.
Composition Type Algebraic Property Resulting Form Canonical Domain
Hierarchical g(R1⋅R2)=g(R1)⋅g(R2)g(R_1 \cdot R_2) = g(R_1) \cdot g(R_2) Power law: f(R)=Rαf(R) = R^{\alpha} AI chain-of-thought (hierarchical abstraction)
Additive f(R1+R2)=f(R1)⋅f(R2)f(R_1 + R_2) = f(R_1) \cdot f(R_2) Exponential: f(R)=ΛRf(R) = \Lambda^R Quantum error correction
Saturating lim⁡R→∞f(R)=fmax\lim_{R \to \infty} f(R) = f_{\max} Logistic: f(R)=fmax1+e−γ(R−R0)f(R) = \frac{f_{\max}}{1 + e^{-\gamma(R - R_0)}} Classical physics (limit cycles)

Important clarification on composition types: The multiplicative Cauchy equation g(R1⋅R2)=g(R1)⋅g(R2)g(R_1 \cdot R_2) = g(R_1) \cdot g(R_2) models hierarchical recursion, where depth levels multiply (e.g., a fractal network with branching factor bb at each of kk levels produces bkb^k total paths). It does not model sequential step-counting, where combining 3 steps and 4 steps yields 7 steps (additive). The power-law form for AI chain-of-thought is therefore more rigorously derived from the Bernoulli ODE (dg/dr=a⋅gβdg/dr = a \cdot g^\beta, which follows from scale invariance) than from the Cauchy functional equation. The Cauchy derivation in Appendix A provides an independent mathematical route to the same power-law solution, but its physical interpretation requires that RR represent hierarchical depth (levels of abstraction) rather than sequential step count. For AI systems where chain-of-thought reasoning builds hierarchical abstractions, this interpretation is plausible but requires empirical validation. We retain both derivations for completeness and note the distinction.

The mathematical derivation (Appendix A) shows that the Cauchy functional equations and the Bernoulli ODE independently yield these functional forms. The composition operator is therefore not merely descriptive but constraining: once we identify the algebraic structure of a domain’s recursive process, the scaling form follows necessarily.

Physical interpretation.

Hierarchical composition models hierarchical or fractal recursion, where each recursive level builds on the structural organisation of the previous level. AI chain-of-thought reasoning, where each reasoning step reinterprets and extends previous insights through increasingly abstract representations, plausibly follows this form. Note that the mathematical derivation (Bernoulli ODE from scale invariance) provides the primary route to the power-law result; the Cauchy functional equation provides an independent derivation valid when RR represents hierarchical depth.

Additive composition models independent error reduction. Each layer contributes a fixed multiplicative reduction in error rate, independent of other layers. Quantum error correction exemplifies this: each increase of two in code distance provides its own protection factor Λ\Lambda, yielding f(R)=ΛRf(R) = \Lambda^R with R=(d+1)/2R = (d+1)/2.

Saturating composition models resource-limited systems where gains diminish as capacity is exhausted. Classical time crystals, whose oscillation settles onto a stable limit cycle (Morrell et al. 2026), exhibit this form.

Key Experimental Test: The composition operator ⊕\oplus is empirically measurable. To determine which scaling law applies to a domain, measure how two sequential recursive blocks compose compared to one block of double depth:

  • If f(2R)=2f(R)f(2R) = 2f(R): scaling is linear (no amplification)

  • If f(2R)=f(R)2f(2R) = f(R)^2: scaling is exponential (additive composition)

  • If f(2R)=2αf(R)f(2R) = 2^{\alpha}f(R): scaling is power-law (multiplicative composition)

This provides a concrete experimental protocol for falsification criterion F10.

Five universal properties: derived theorems.

Within the formalism, five structural properties follow from the composition operator; several are elementary consequences of the definitions, stated as theorems for reference rather than for depth. Whether every domain that shows recursive amplification shares them is the empirical question F4 tests:

The Five Universal Properties (Derived from ⊕\oplus):

Theorem 1 (Threshold behaviour). A critical coupling strength β*\beta^* exists below which recursive gains vanish.

Derivation. For any composition operator ⊕\oplus, if δQr∝βQr\delta Q_r \propto \beta Q_r, then Qr+1=Qr(1+β)Q_{r+1} = Q_r(1 + \beta). For β<0\beta < 0, gains become losses; the system decays. The threshold β*=0\beta^* = 0 marks the boundary between amplification and attenuation. For power-law scaling, α=1/(1−β)>1\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) > 1 requires β>0\beta > 0. ◻

Theorem 2 (Recursive depth dependence). Capability increases with self-referential cycles (RR), not merely parallel resources.

Derivation. The composition operator ⊕\oplus operates sequentially: Qr+1=Qr⊕δQrQ_{r+1} = Q_r \oplus \delta Q_r. Each step depends on the previous output. Parallel resources increase II (the base) but do not increase RR (the recursive depth). The multiplicative structure I×f(R)I \times f(R) separates these contributions. ◻

Theorem 3 (Base quality dependence). The system requires structured asymmetry (I>0I > 0); without it, recursion has nothing to amplify.

Derivation. If I=0I = 0, then U=0×f(R)=0U = 0 \times f(R) = 0 for any RR. The composition operator amplifies what exists; it cannot create from nothing. This is the II-irreducibility theorem. ◻

Theorem 4 (Multiplicative I×RI \times R interaction). Base quality and recursive depth interact multiplicatively, not additively. The multiplicative structure is necessary, not merely convenient.

Proof by contradiction. Suppose U=p(I)+q(R)U = p(I) + q(R) for some functions p,qp, q. From Axiom 1, U(I,0)=IU(I, 0) = I, so p(I)+q(0)=Ip(I) + q(0) = I, giving p(I)=I−q(0)p(I) = I - q(0). But from the corrected Axiom 2, U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R) where g(R)g(R) satisfies dg/dR=a⋅gβdg/dR = a \cdot g^\beta independently of II. Substituting: I×g(R)=I+[q(R)−q(0)]I \times g(R) = I + [q(R) - q(0)], which gives g(R)=1+[q(R)−q(0)]/Ig(R) = 1 + [q(R) - q(0)]/I. The right side depends on II, but g(R)g(R) is defined as a function of RR alone. Contradiction. ◻

Note: The corrected formulation (ODE on gg rather than UU) eliminates the Iβ−1I^{\beta-1} dependence that arose in the original proof, making the separation of II and g(R)g(R) exact rather than asymptotic. The multiplicative structure U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R) is a direct consequence of the axioms, not an approximation.

Proof note (24 October 2026). The proof shows that no additive decomposition U=p(I)+q(R)U = p(I) + q(R) is consistent with the multiplicative form U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R) together with the growth law dg/dR=agβdg/dR = a\,g^{\beta}; it does not derive the multiplicative form from weaker premises, since it assumes it. The growth law is Appendix A’s Axiom 3, printed above as Axiom 2, as it is in Theorem 6 and in Table 27’s row on blind prediction testing, and U(I,0)=IU(I, 0) = I uses the initial condition g(0)=1g(0) = 1 of Appendix A.2, not Axiom 1’s g(1)=1g(1) = 1. Unchanged: the theorem’s statement, read as a statement about these axioms.

Theorem 5 (Regime boundaries). Systems exhibit qualitatively different behaviour above and below critical thresholds.

Derivation. The composition operator determines the functional form within the stated model. In the solution U(R)=I[1+(a/α)R]αU(R)=I[1+(a/\alpha)R]^\alpha, the balance of terms changes smoothly around the characteristic scale R*=α/aR^*=\alpha/a. This is a crossover, not a discontinuity. The limit β→1\beta\to1 changes the power-law family to an exponential on the original depth coordinate. Appendix A.3 distinguishes the characteristic scale from a crossing of unit elasticity. ◻

Derivation note (24 October 2026). In the solution of Section 4.4, U(R)=I×[1+(a/α)R]αU(R) = I \times [1 + (a/\alpha)R]^{\alpha}, the change of dominant term is a change of regime in scaling behaviour: a smooth crossover, not a discontinuity or a phase transition. Unchanged: the theorem’s statement.

These five properties constitute the qualitative ARC Principle. Their derivation from the composition operator ensures internal consistency: accepting the formalism commits one to all five properties. The specific functional form is an empirical question for each domain; the properties are theorems.

4.2 The AI-specific form: power-law scaling

For AI systems exhibiting multiplicative composition, the generalised equation in the deep recursion regime (R≫R*R \gg R^*) reduces to:

U≈I×Rα\begin{equation*} U \approx I \times R^{\alpha} \end{equation*}(5) Effective capability == Base potential ×\times Recursive depthα^{\alpha} (deep recursion limit)

The exact integrated form, derived in Section 4.4, is U(R)=I×[1+aαR]αU(R) = I \times [1 + \frac{a}{\alpha}R]^{\alpha}. The pure power law is its asymptotic limit when recursive depth substantially exceeds the characteristic scale R*R^*. Neither R*R^* nor that regime has been identified by the AI error-decay fits reported here. Applying those fits to the capability model requires the metric and coordinate conditions of Section 5.2.1; Appendix A.3 gives the finite-depth elasticity.

In plain language: Effective capability (UU) equals the starting potential (II) multiplied by the recursive depth (RR) raised to a power (α\alpha) that depends on how well each step builds on the previous one.

4.3 What each variable means

UU: effective capability.

What the system actually achieves. Measured differently in each domain:

  • AI: A declared benchmark measure, such as accuracy; inverse error is a different, explicitly chosen proxy (Section 5.2.1)

  • Quantum: Logical qubit fidelity (how error-free the computation is)

  • Physics: Temporal stability of the time crystal

  • Biology: Metabolic efficiency (thermodynamic) or cognitive task performance (behavioural)

II: base potential (structured asymmetry).

Thermodynamic definition: Natural systems tend towards maximum entropy (equilibrium/uniformity). In this framework, “artificial” denotes any system maintaining low-entropy structure against the thermodynamic gradient, whether engineered (an AI model), evolved (a brain), or emergent (a time crystal). The parameter II measures how far from maximum entropy the system starts.

In Morrell, Elliott and Grier’s experiment, identical beads interact reciprocally and no active region exists: “The active region vanishes for particles of the same size (a1=a2a_1 = a_2), whose interactions are reciprocal” (Morrell et al. 2026). The framework reads this as an instance of its zero-factor property, a correspondence of structure and not a test. Order requires designed disorder: a specific pattern of asymmetry that enables work extraction from the environment.

Table 3. What the base potential II measures in each domain, and its physical meaning.
Domain What II measures Physical meaning
AI Single-pass value of the chosen task metric Baseline on that same metric; accuracy and inverse error are not interchangeable
Quantum Raw qubit quality (1−1 - error rate) Distance from maximum entropy
Physics Variance in bead sizes Asymmetry enabling nonreciprocal forces
Biology Initial learning rate Sensitivity gradient

The Constraint Principle: Constraint enables competence. Without structured asymmetry, no work can be extracted. The time-crystal case above is the physical correspondence; criterion F3 grades it a correspondence of structure, not a test (Table 21).

RR: recursive depth.

How many self-referential cycles the system performs. The output of cycle nn becomes the input for cycle n+1n+1.

Quantum One step of two in code distance Code distance dd, with R=(d+1)/2R = (d+1)/2

Critical requirement: For α>1\alpha > 1, recursion must incorporate sequential self-correction: each step building on previous outputs. Pure parallel processing (independent attempts averaged together) cannot achieve α>1\alpha > 1 because it lacks the output→\toinput feedback loop. However, hybrid parallel-sequential approaches may achieve intermediate scaling (Li et al. 2025).

α\alpha: the scaling exponent.

The scaling exponent determines the system’s scaling regime:

α<1\alpha < 1 Diminishing returns Parallel voting: more samples help less and less
α=1\alpha = 1 Linear returns Each step adds a fixed amount
α>1\alpha > 1 Compounding returns Each step multiplies capability

Our core prediction: αsequential>1>αparallel\alpha_{\text{sequential}} > 1 > \alpha_{\text{parallel}}

4.4 Deriving α\alpha from first principles

This derivation completes the paper’s theoretical contribution. Without it, α\alpha is just a number we fit to data. With it, α\alpha becomes a predictable quantity.

The key insight.

How much does your accumulated knowledge help your next step?

Define β∈[0,1)\beta \in [0, 1) as the “self-referential coupling”: how much of accumulated context each new step can effectively leverage. When β=0.5\beta = 0.5, each step benefits from half of accumulated context. The domain restriction β<1\beta < 1 is essential: at β=1\beta = 1, the ODE solution diverges (α→∞\alpha \to \infty), producing a finite-time singularity that no physical system can realise.

Derivation note (19 September 2026). An owner review of the reason given for the domain restriction finds that the restriction is right and that the reason printed for it is not, and this note replaces the reason while keeping the restriction. With the governing equation dg/dr=agβdg/dr = a\,g^{\beta} of this section and the initial condition g(0)=1g(0) = 1 used in Appendix A.2, the case β=1\beta = 1 gives dg/dr=agdg/dr = a\,g and hence g(R)=eaRg(R) = e^{aR}, which is finite at every finite depth: the solution there is exponential, not singular. For β≠1\beta \ne 1, integrating g−βdg=adrg^{-\beta}dg = a\,dr under the same initial condition gives g1−β=1+a(1−β)Rg^{1-\beta} = 1 + a(1-\beta)R. The finite-depth branch is therefore β>1\beta > 1, where that reads g−(β−1)=1−a(β−1)Rg^{-(\beta-1)} = 1 - a(\beta-1)R, which reaches zero at the finite depth R*=1/[a(β−1)]R^{*} = 1/[a(\beta-1)], and gg diverges there. The two statements inside the parenthesis above are also separate statements. As β\beta rises towards 1 from below the exponent α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) does diverge, while the solution converges pointwise to the exponential, since [1+a(1−β)R]1/(1−β)→eaR[1 + a(1-\beta)R]^{1/(1-\beta)} \to e^{aR}; at a=1a = 1 and R=3R = 3 the solution is 13.79 at β=0.9\beta = 0.9, 19.22 at β=0.99\beta = 0.99 and 20.00 at β=0.999\beta = 0.999, against e3=20.09e^{3} = 20.09. A diverging exponent is not a diverging solution. The domain β∈[0,1)\beta \in [0,1), printed here and again in Appendix A.2, stands unchanged, on the ground that it is what makes α\alpha finite and the power-law form exist at all. The plain-language gloss in the second sentence is scoped in the same way: from the governing equation, log⁡(dg/dr)=log⁡a+βlog⁡g\log(dg/dr) = \log a + \beta\log g, so β\beta is the log elasticity of marginal gain with respect to accumulated amplification, which is exactly the quantity the computational validation below measures from marginal gains in log-log space. A fraction of accumulated context, or of tokens, is a different quantity and would need its own operational definition before the gloss could be read literally. Unchanged: the domain restriction, the exact integrated solution, the identity α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta), and the validation result reported below.

If each step is independent (β=0\beta = 0), you get linear scaling (α=1\alpha = 1).
If each step fully leverages all prior work (β→1\beta \to 1), scaling explodes.

The mathematics.

Since U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R), the compounding operates on the amplification factor g(R)g(R), not on the absolute capability UU. The marginal amplification gained at step rr depends on accumulated amplification:

dgdr=a×gβ\begin{equation*} \frac{dg}{dr} = a \times g^{\beta} \end{equation*}(6)

Why this form? This differential equation models cumulative advantage (also called preferential attachment; Barabási and Albert 1999): the rate of amplification gain is proportional to the system’s current amplification raised to a power. Critically, the ODE operates on gg (the amplification factor) rather than UU (the absolute capability), ensuring that the base intelligence II acts purely as a multiplicative starting constant and does not contaminate the recursive dynamics. This resolves an algebraic inconsistency present in earlier versions of this paper (see Ledger Note 1 in the Version history (Appendix B.6)).

Solving this differential equation (details in Appendix A) with initial condition g(0)=1g(0) = 1 yields:

U(R)=I×[1+aαR]αwhereα=11−β\begin{equation*} U(R) = I \times \left[ 1 + \frac{a}{\alpha} R \right]^{\alpha} \quad \text{where} \quad \alpha = \frac{1}{1 - \beta} \end{equation*}(7) The corrected ARC equation (exact integrated form)

In the deep recursion limit (R≫α/aR \gg \alpha/a), this simplifies to U≈I×RαU \approx I \times R^{\alpha}, recovering the power-law form used throughout the empirical sections of this paper.

Coefficient note (19 September 2026). An owner review of this limit finds that the approximate equality above drops a coefficient that this paper’s own appendix keeps, and this note restores it. For (a/α)R≫1(a/\alpha)R \gg 1 the bracket in the exact solution tends to (a/α)R(a/\alpha)R, so U(R)→I(a/α)αRαU(R) \to I\,(a/\alpha)^{\alpha}R^{\alpha}. That factor is not near one in general: it is 0.25 at α=2\alpha = 2 with a=1a = 1, 0.0625 at α=2\alpha = 2 with a=0.5a = 0.5, 0.68 at α=1.33\alpha = 1.33 with a=1a = 1, and 0.037 at α=3\alpha = 3 with a=1a = 1. Appendix A.2 already prints both correct forms, the proportionality U∝IRαU \propto I\,R^{\alpha} and the explicit U≈I(a/α)αRαU \approx I\,(a/\alpha)^{\alpha}R^{\alpha}, and the sentence above is to be read as that proportionality. The coefficient may not be absorbed into II: it is built from the recursion parameters aa and α\alpha, and the note on the corrected formulation in this section, repeated in Appendix A.2, puts the differential equation on the amplification factor precisely so that II remains a multiplicative constant outside the recursive dynamics. Where an amplitude is fitted to data instead, the fitted amplitude is I(a/α)αI\,(a/\alpha)^{\alpha} and not the II of that note. Unchanged: the exact integrated solution; the empirical sections, which fit exponents rather than amplitudes, so no reported result depends on the dropped factor; and the crossover depth R*=α/aR^{*} = \alpha/a.
