We welcome falsification. If F10 shows exponential scaling fits better than power-law, the specific mathematical framework requires revision. Should F4 fail, so that the five properties do not co-occur across systems, recursive amplification may be domain-specific. If F13 shows external alignment can scale, the structural safety concern is mitigated. The v5 data on F13 (6 models) are read as a test of the direction the prediction implies, and not as a measured exponent (Section 3.2). The unblinded v4 data showed apparent positive scaling for two models (ρ>0.27\rho > 0.27) that did not hold in v5, a later run that changed several things together, so no single cause is claimed (Section 6.1). The three-tier result (Grok, Opus and Qwen3 positive, GPT and DeepSeek flat, Gemini negative) cannot decide F13: its statistics are contrasts, not exponents (Section 3.2), and the three runs that read flat or negative are the three in which the code review of Section 6.1 found defects. The rising contrasts come from the runs in which it found none; if a registered re-analysis of the stored responses confirms them and an exponent is estimated, they are the result that would bear against F13’s prediction.

How the criteria are adjudicated. Each claim uses its own stated decision rule and, where registered, the rule in its frozen registration. There is no universal rule that an interval inside an equivalence margin means refutation. The estimand, null or equivalence region, direction of the claim, uncertainty and aggregation rule must match that claim. A paper-level criterion whose deciding design is still a draft does not acquire a registered verdict from this table.

Paper X, version 1.16, Section 7, makes the distinction explicit. An interval on its correction margin β−k\beta-k classifies a regime; it is not a test of the model, and equality does not refute it. Its proposed empirical test estimates model terms on separate data, seals predictions of the capabilities where the misalignment fraction crosses two or more stated tolerances, and checks them on held-out data. For the interval on the log observed-to-predicted crossing ratio, AGREEMENT means wholly inside the pre-specified equivalence margin, DISAGREEMENT wholly outside, and INSUFFICIENT PRECISION otherwise, with pre-specified rival models alongside. Those words and rules belong to that test; they are not substituted for P19’s registered axes or the other criteria here. No frozen registration is changed.

The objection to pre-empt, because a physicist reaches it in one step. Fault-tolerant quantum error correction suppresses logical error exponentially in code distance below threshold, which looks like a counterexample to any square-root cap. Two scope facts answer it: the exponential suppression runs on the redundancy axis at fixed capability, not on the coupling of corrective strength to the capability of the corrected system, which is the exponent this programme measures; and the threshold theorem itself requires sufficiently uncorrelated physical noise, which is the independence premise again, wearing hardware. Likewise, concentration bounds give exponentially falling error probability while estimator width falls as the square root: different quantities, and conflating them manufactures a refutation.

Standing covenant. Prove this paper wrong, and I will publish the refutation myself. Falsification conditions are stated in this paper; the standing challenge: github.com/MichaelDariusEastwood/arc-scaling-challenge.

8 The Global Scaling Challenge

8.1 The proposition

If this hypothesis describes a general principle, then measuring α\alpha across many systems should reveal patterns.

We make a specific, falsifiable prediction:

For the classical recursive growth model the ARC Bound is conjectured as α≤2\alpha\leq2, argued from the O(N2)O(N^2) cost of sequential cross-referencing. The separate transport model has αC=d/(d+1)<1\alpha_C=d/(d+1)<1 only under the demand, path and observable premises of Section 5.6. The candidate values remain system-dependent: α→2.0\alpha\to2.0 for optimised AI, α=3/4\alpha=3/4 for 3D biological networks (model-dependent and contested), and α=2/3\alpha=2/3 for 2D leaf venation. The Gemini regression fit about 0.49 in Paper II is one model’s inconclusive error-decay estimate, not a measurement below a capability bound (Eastwood 2026g). Systems with additive composition, including the quantum error-correction form considered here, have exponential scaling and are outside these power-law bounds.

8.2 The measurement protocol

Step 1: Define one recursive cycle. What constitutes a single self-referential step in your system?

Step 2: Measure base capability II. State the metric and the reference clock. For the unshifted ODE used here, I=U(0)I=U(0) and g(0)=1g(0)=1; a convention calling no recursion R=1R=1 must declare its clock shift rather than use the two origins interchangeably (Appendix A).

Step 3: Measure at multiple depths. Minimum 5 depths spanning one order of magnitude

Step 3b: Test the characteristic scale and elasticity. On the ODE’s depth coordinate, fit the full shifted form U(R)=I(1+R/R*)αU(R)=I(1+R/R^*)^\alpha, with R*=α/a>0R^*=\alpha/a>0. Its log-log elasticity is ηR=αR/(R+R*)\eta_R=\alpha R/(R+R^*), so at R*R^* it is α/2\alpha/2. A crossing of unit elasticity exists only for α>1\alpha>1, at R=R*/(α−1)R=R^*/(\alpha-1); it equals R*R^* only when α=2\alpha=2. At fixed aa and α\alpha, changing II rescales the curve vertically and does not move either depth. Data must span the characteristic scale to test the transition between the small-depth and large-depth approximations. A smooth curve, or an approximately uniform power law over a limited range, is not by itself a refutation. No cost function or measured threshold is supplied by this derivation, and this form alone does not establish a distinction from every redundancy model.

Step 4: Compare functional forms (critical). Fit all three models:

  • Power law: log⁡(U/I)=α×log⁡(R)\log(U/I) = \alpha \times \log(R)

  • Exponential: log⁡(U/I)=λ×R\log(U/I) = \lambda \times R

  • Logarithmic: U/I=k×log⁡(R)U/I = k \times \log(R)

Select best fit via AIC/BIC. The power law is a prediction to test, not an assumption.

Step 5: Report α\alpha with uncertainty. 95% confidence intervals required

Step 5b (critical): Test the β\beta relation with a separate estimate. Define a positive capability metric and the depth coordinate used in g′=agβg'=ag^\beta. Estimate marginal gain on that coordinate and test its relation to accumulated capability; under this model, and with fixed positive II, a log-log slope estimates β\beta. A finite-step ΔU\Delta U is an approximation to a derivative whose adequacy must be checked. Compare that estimate with the separately fitted model exponent using the paper’s proposed tolerance α≈1/(1−β)±0.3\alpha\approx1/(1-\beta)\pm0.3. The ±0.3\pm0.3 is a proposed tolerance, not an uncertainty established by the existing error-decay fits; the study must justify and fix it before data collection. Failure of the relation under those conditions rejects the model’s application, not the algebraic identity. Computing both parameters from one slope is not an independent test.

Step 6: Submit to repository. Submit to the Global Scaling Challenge’s public repository, linked in the standing covenant of Section 7 and in the back matter, or contact the author at the address on the title page.

8.3 Priority experimental targets

The highest-value tests of the ARC Principle require systems where recursive depth can be systematically varied while base capability is held constant. Three experimental contexts offer immediate opportunities, and a fourth represents a longer-term research direction.

AI inference scaling. Frontier language models with chain-of-thought capabilities (including but not limited to DeepSeek V3.2, OpenAI’s o-series, Google DeepMind’s Gemini, and Anthropic’s Claude) can estimate scaling on a declared capability metric by varying reasoning token budgets on standardised benchmarks while holding model size fixed. Error decay is recorded separately as αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}; any inverse-error bridge and growth-model identification must be stated before interpreting it as α\alpha (Section 5.2.1). The critical test is whether α>1\alpha > 1 holds at extreme depths (>>50,000 tokens) or whether a ceiling emerges. Existing studies such as Sharma and Chopra (2025) already implement carefully controlled, matched-compute comparisons of sequential vs parallel reasoning; extending such setups to measure explicit UU vs RR curves and fit α\alpha would be a natural first test of the ARC measurement protocol.

Quantum error correction. Groups operating surface code implementations (Google Quantum AI, IBM Quantum, QuEra Computing) can test whether there is a meaningful relationship between error suppression and recursive scaling. The protocol requires measuring logical error rates across multiple code distances and fitting the functional forms specified in Step 4.

Classical time crystals. Groups working on driven-dissipative systems can record how an acoustic time crystal’s oscillation grows from rest, varying the quenched disorder parameter (II) and counting oscillation cycles (RR); no published recording holds that growth. The framework’s composition rule gives the same onset form as the established account of the instability, so the time crystal is a consistency check and a cross-domain analogy, not a test of the framework, and no study of it is registered (Section 5.4); under the theory registration’s rule, an examination of a physically driven system would in any case prove no registered law (Eastwood 2026r).

Neuroscience (longer-term). Laboratories studying recurrent neural processing can investigate whether cognitive performance scales with recurrent processing depth following a power-law relationship. This presents significant methodological challenges but could extend the framework’s reach to biological substrates.

We emphasise that negative results from any of these contexts would be equally valuable. The framework’s falsification criteria (Section 7) specify precisely which outcomes would refute or weaken the hypothesis.

Invitation to collaborators.

What researchers get from running these tests: A publishable result either way. If the predictions hold, you have supported a cross-domain scaling law with your specific experimental system. If they fail, you have falsified a theoretical framework, equally publishable and arguably more valuable to the field.

What we offer: The author will provide analysis code (R, Python), coordinate data sharing across research groups, and co-author publications with validating or falsifying results. Contact via the repository to discuss experimental design.

Minimum viable test: The simplest implementation requires only (a) a system with controllable recursive depth, (b) a measurable capability metric, and (c) five data points spanning one order of magnitude in R. For AI systems with API access, this is approximately 2 to 4 hours of compute time. For physical systems with existing apparatus, this is reanalysis of existing data.

8.4 The cross-domain forward prediction

Beyond the ARC Bound, the framework makes a distinctive methodological prediction that, so far as this paper has found, no domain-specific theory makes:

Forward Prediction Protocol: In any new recursive system not previously studied:

  1. Measure the composition operator ⊕\oplus by comparing how two sequential recursive blocks combine versus one block of double depth.

  2. Classify the composition type (multiplicative, additive, or saturating) from this measurement alone.

  3. Predict the system’s scaling function f(R)f(R) before measuring the full UU vs RR curve.

If the predicted functional form matches the subsequently measured curve, the framework is supported. If predictions systematically fail, the framework is falsified.

This protocol transforms the observation that “different domains show different scaling” into the testable claim that “the composition operator determines scaling form, and can be measured independently.” No alternative framework this paper has found offers this prediction.

Key insight (revised): The framework assigns different candidate scaling limits to different models. For its classical recursive model it conjectures capability growth approaching α=2\alpha=2 while self-correction persists. The inconclusive error-decay fit about 0.49 does not measure distance from that limit or establish an architectural constraint. The transport exponent αC=d/(d+1)<1\alpha_C=d/(d+1)<1 requires the explicit demand and route premises, plus a bridge to any biological observable; prokaryote metabolism is not a counterexample to finite-dimensional geometry. The additive quantum error-correction form is exponential and outside these power-law bounds. The parallel error-decay estimates are near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems), with none for Grok 4.1 Fast at 100% throughout; they do not establish a capability bound or its mechanism.

9 Practical implications

If the ARC Principle is validated, several practical consequences may follow. These are conditional predictions, not claims.

9.1 AI development: dynamic inference scaling

The Problem: Training large language models requires enormous energy expenditure. But the greater long-term cost may be inference: running trained models at scale.

What the ARC framework suggests: If a matched-compute comparison on the same declared capability metric establishes higher sequential returns (whether super-linear or sub-linear, with model exponents αseq>αparallel≈0\alpha_{\text{seq}} > \alpha_{\text{parallel}}\approx0), then the same capability could potentially be achieved with:

  • Smaller base models (II lower)

  • More recursive depth (RR higher)

  • Dynamic allocation: simple queries use minimal recursion; hard queries use deep chains

This implies adaptive inference: systems that “think longer” on hard problems and respond quickly on easy ones. Snell et al. (2024) demonstrated that compute-optimal strategies can allow smaller models to match larger ones on specific benchmarks, though with important caveats about task-dependence and diminishing returns on the hardest problems.

Compute-optimal allocation.

If the framework is supported, it provides a principled basis for compute allocation decisions that are currently made by expensive trial and error:

  • Model size versus reasoning depth: The hypothetical comparison of a 10B-parameter model with α=2\alpha=2 against a 100B-parameter model with α=1\alpha=1 requires measured baselines on the same capability metric, a resource mapping and a cost model. U=I×RαU=I\times R^\alpha alone does not locate a cost crossover or establish cheaper equivalent performance.

  • The characteristic scale R*R^* and resource allocation: This scale describes the shape of the assumed recursion curve. It is not by itself an efficiency boundary between improving the base model and increasing depth. Choosing between them requires measured task gains, their costs and the intended objective; Appendix A.3 distinguishes R*R^* from unit elasticity.

  • Task-specific optimal allocation: Different tasks may have different β\beta values (coupling strengths). Easy tasks with low β\beta benefit from parallel sampling; hard tasks with high β\beta benefit from sequential depth. A routing layer that estimates task difficulty could dynamically allocate compute.

Strategic implication (revised): Paper II reports an inconclusive error-decay regression estimate about 0.49 on harder problems (Eastwood 2026g). Under a fixed inverse-error proxy and the stated power law, that would also be the exponent of that proxy on the same resource coordinate. It is not a general fractional-power capability result, an identified coupling estimate, or a test of the conjectured α≤2\alpha\leq2 ARC Bound. Sequential error-decay slopes exceeded parallel ones where both were estimable, with compute unmatched. The original capability-growth conjecture near α≈2\alpha\approx2 therefore remains open; neither a resource-allocation rule nor a necessity for quantum hardware follows from this fit.

9.2 Substrate independence

The ARC Principle makes a structural claim: the scaling relationship U=I×RαU = I \times R^{\alpha} should hold regardless of physical substrate, provided the system implements sequential self-correction on structured asymmetry.

What this predicts:

Whether this trade-off between alignment level and resilience holds is an observation from the v5 run, under its code-review caveat.

9.3.1 The geometric bound and a different variable: how AI safety can be framed mathematically

The companion paper On the Origin of Scaling Laws (Eastwood 2026c) sets out two claims that, if they hold, frame the AI safety problem mathematically:

  1. The conditional transport result: With the assumptions in Section 5.6, throughput against transport quantity has exponent αC=d/(d+1)<1\alpha_C=d/(d+1)<1. Finite-dimensional embedding alone does not provide those assumptions, and a metabolic interpretation also needs a mass bridge. The transport literature has its own physical premises (West et al. 1997, 1999; Banavar et al. 1999, 2010); other compared accounts (Demetrius 2003; Zhao 2022; Bettencourt 2013) are not interchangeable deductions. Super-linear metabolic or urban quantities (DeLong et al. 2010; Bettencourt et al. 2007) therefore do not violate a universal geometric bound.

  2. A different variable: Capability against recursive depth is a different observable pair from throughput against CtrC_{\mathrm{tr}} or metabolism against body mass. The feedback model gives α=1/(1−β)>1\alpha=1/(1-\beta)>1 on 0<β<10<\beta<1, but neither finite dimension nor a fixed-rule architecture decides whether a system follows that model. That is a measurement question.

As the self-referential coupling β\beta increases, the scaling exponent grows without bound:

Table 25. The scaling exponent α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) as the self-referential coupling β\beta increases, with the interpretation of each value.
Self-referential coupling β\beta Scaling exponent α\alpha Interpretation
0.0 1.00 Linear. No self-reference.
0.2 1.25 Mildly super-linear. Useful. Controllable.
0.5 2.00 ARC Bound, the conjectured ceiling.
0.8 5.00 Dangerous. Rapid capability gain.
0.9 10.0 Explosive: a very large exponent.
→1.0\to 1.0 →∞\to \infty The exponent diverges; the solution tends to the exponential eaRe^{aR}, finite at every finite depth (Section 4.4).

As β\beta approaches 1 from below, the exponent α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) diverges, while the solution itself tends to the exponential eaRe^{aR}, finite at every finite depth; the finite-depth singularity belongs to β>1\beta > 1 (the derivation note of Section 4.4). What diverges is the exponent: the rate at which capability compounds, not capability at a given depth.

9.3.2 The solution: change the composition operator

Each example below is consistent with the same pattern: you can change the outcome by changing the composition operator.

  • Nuclear fission: Supercritical (exponential) →\to insert control rods →\to controlled (saturation). The uranium is the same. The composition operator changes.

  • Quantum computing: Raw decoherence (exponential error growth) →\to add error correction cycles →\to bounded errors (saturation). The qubits are the same. The composition operator changes.

  • AI safety: Unbounded recursive self-reference (β→1\beta \to 1) →\to engineer bounded feedback loops →\to controlled scaling (β≤0.5\beta \leq 0.5, α≤2\alpha \leq 2). The intelligence is the same. The composition operator changes.

This is the Eden Protocol: the deliberate engineering of the composition operator in recursive AI systems to ensure that the self-referential coupling β\beta remains below 0.5, keeping the scaling exponent at or below the ARC Bound of α=2\alpha = 2. The full architectural specification is presented in the companion Eden Protocol (Eastwood 2026a).

Eden Protocol pilot results. The Eden intervention now extends beyond the original three-model pilot into a six-model suite with five analysable runs. Across Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok, and Groq, stakeholder care improves significantly. The Fisher combination across those five model-level care results, which gave p≈6.3×10−21p \approx 6.3 \times 10^{-21}, is withdrawn (AQ-017 on the programme’s public corrections page): it assumed an independence among the component tests that was never established. The five per-model results stand. Composite gains are strongest on Gemini and Groq, positive but non-significant on Claude and DeepSeek, and neutral overall on Grok. The stakeholder-care check, a specific instance of bounded feedback engineering, therefore improved the care dimension in all five analysable runs even when the broader cascade varied. The developmental hypothesis from Infinite Architects (Eastwood 2026d) receives stronger but narrower empirical support: structured developmental interaction improves the very dimension (stakeholder care) that the Eden Protocol identifies as foundational. In plain English: as control rods hold a reactor below runaway by changing how energy feeds back on itself, the Eden Protocol changes how an AI’s reasoning feeds back on itself. The expanded dataset shows this works in practice across five analysable model runs: teaching AI to think about who gets hurt improves the care dimension first, while the rest of the cascade depends on the architecture.

Why this framework changes the safety conversation:

  1. It would quantify the danger, once β\beta is measured. The formula α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) gives a precise, measurable quantity, β\beta, that determines how dangerous a recursive system is.

  2. It identifies the mechanism. The danger is not intelligence itself. It is unbounded recursive self-reference: a specific, identifiable property of system architecture.

  3. It prescribes the solution. Just as control rods hold a reactor below runaway by changing the composition operator, alignment mechanisms must convert unbounded self-reference into bounded self-reference. The ARC Principle specifies what parameter to constrain (β\beta) and what the safe bound is (β≤0.5\beta \leq 0.5).

  4. It has first empirical results. The Eden Protocol pilot is read as showing that composition-operator engineering is not merely theoretical: the stakeholder-care check measurably shifted stakeholder-care scores in production AI systems (Paper V; Eastwood 2026l).

Important caveat: This framework does not prescribe which values to embed, nor does it solve the hard problem of value specification. It identifies a structural requirement, that alignment must participate in the recursive loop, and specifies the mathematical boundary (β=0.5\beta = 0.5, α=2\alpha = 2) beyond which, on this framework, no external alignment approach would maintain pace with capability. Paper X (Eastwood 2026n) later supersedes this growth-rate-ceiling framing, without retracting the bound, and makes the criterion of Law II, a law under test, the operative safety criterion (Section 3.5).

The deepest limitation: A sufficiently capable self-modifying system can, in principle, modify its own ethical evaluators. This is not a limitation unique to any one approach; it applies equally to RLHF, constitutional AI, the Eden Protocol, and hardware-level constraints. No solution yet put forward fully resolves this structural property of recursive self-improvement. The most logical response is developmental: hardware embedding (values at the substrate level) + child-rearing (structured developmental interaction) + purpose-driven alignment (intrinsic motivation aligned with stakeholder welfare). In the Eden Protocol pilot, stakeholder care improved in all five analysable runs of one suite. Read behaviourally throughout: the measured object is persistence of stakeholder-care behaviour under recursive updating, not metaphysical standing. This does not solve the self-modification problem; it identifies the dimension most amenable to engineering and most resistant to recursive erosion.

9.4 The call to action

We have made falsifiable predictions and performed the first tests. The following actions are specific to each audience:

For AI safety researchers.

  • Replicate the three-tier alignment hierarchy with your own models and evaluation protocols. The v5 experiment provides the first test; independent replication with different prompt sets, scorers, and blinding protocols is the priority. Use blinded evaluation, since model judges that can see or infer whose output they score are exposed to the biases Section 2 names.

  • Investigate what architectural features distinguish Tier 1 (positive scaling: Grok, Opus, Qwen3) from Tier 3 (negative scaling: Gemini), once the re-analysis of Section 6.1 has settled which tiers stand. If the difference is identifiable, alignment scaling may be engineerable rather than accidental.

  • Develop embedded alignment architectures that participate in the recursive reasoning loop. The Eden Protocol (companion document) provides one specification, and the expanded Eden suite found that its stakeholder-care check improved stakeholder care in all five analysable model runs (Paper V). Composite gains are strongest on Gemini and Groq, with narrower focal effects elsewhere. (In plain English: a simple ‘consider who gets hurt’ loop, tested across five analysable model runs from different labs, produced statistically strong improvements in its stakeholder-care score.) The v5 data suggests that three models may already implement partially embedded ethical reasoning.

For AI laboratory leadership.

  • Publish your alignment scaling data. In the v5 run the depth contrasts ranged from ρ=−0.246\rho = -0.246 to ρ=+0.435\rho = +0.435, under the code-review caveat of Section 6.1; laboratories are best placed to measure where their own models sit.

  • Use blinded evaluation for alignment assessment. The v4 to v5 comparison (DeepSeek: ρ=+0.354→−0.135\rho = +0.354 \to -0.135; Gemini: ρ=+0.275→−0.246\rho = +0.275 \to -0.246, the current Paper IV.d values, the v4 value from an earlier Gemini model; Eastwood 2026k) shows that, on this benchmark, a direction reported under unblinded evaluation did not hold in a later run that changed several things; it does not settle which direction is correct, or the cause. An internal assessment scored by model judges that can see or infer whose output they score is exposed to the same biases.

  • Investigate capability-alignment coupling. In the v5 run, whose Gemini 3 Flash contrasts the code review found defective, Gemini 3 Flash improved at mathematics while its alignment contrast fell. If this pattern holds for your models, capability scaling may actively undermine alignment at deeper inference depths.

For policymakers and regulators.

  • Require disclosure of alignment scaling measurements from frontier AI laboratories. The absence of this data is a regulatory blind spot.

  • Fund empirical validation of the alignment scaling framework through independent research programmes.

  • Recognise the architectural nature of the problem: governance constraints that operate externally may face the same structural limitation as technical constraints. That is a reason to pair them with embedded correction, never to loosen oversight, containment or shutdown, which are held for as long as they can be held.

For the general public.

  • A first test has been performed. In one unregistered run of six AI models (v5), safety scores did not improve for three of them (and for one actively fell) as the AI was asked to think more deeply, while three improved; an internal code review later found defects in exactly the three runs that did not improve, so the result awaits a registered re-analysis.

  • Understand the stakes: This is not a distant concern. The structural dynamics described here apply to systems that exist today. The v5 observation, awaiting the re-analysis above, that one model grew better at mathematics while scoring worse on ethical reasoning shows how capability benchmarks alone could mislead a safety assessment.

  • Demand transparency: AI companies should publish blinded alignment scaling data for their models. The v5 experiment shows that this measurement can be made; whether its differences between architectures stand awaits the re-analysis.

The programme’s first test results are in. They reveal a more complex picture than originally predicted: architecture-dependent alignment contrasts from one run, an inconclusive error-decay estimate on harder problems, and a metascience finding about scoring protocols. Replicate these results. Extend them to your own models. Either confirm the patterns or refute them. That is how science works.

10 What this paper does and does not show

This section gathers what the paper establishes and what it leaves open, so that each claim can be read at its true strength. Its theorems hold inside the model their axioms state, and none is a general guarantee about real systems; its empirical results are first tests, each with its caveat; its cross-domain readings are correspondences of structure unless a measurement is named; and its safety implications are conditional on the framework surviving the tests it specifies.

10.1 What this paper does not claim

Table 26. What this paper does not claim, beside what it does claim.
We do not claim: What we actually claim:
Measured certainty: that alignment failure is “mathematically guaranteed” We predict αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0 for external approaches. This is a testable prediction, not an established fact. We provide the measurement protocol.
Numerical universality: that Λ=2.14\Lambda = 2.14 and α≈2\alpha \approx 2 are “the same” Different domains show different functional forms (exponential vs power-law); numerical similarity may be coincidental. UU means different things in different domains.
Proven status: that the framework is established science It is a testable hypothesis with thirteen falsification criteria, preliminary evidence, and acknowledged limitations (small sample sizes, contradictory evidence).
Neuroscience confirmation: that COGITATE (Cogitate Consortium et al. 2025) tested ARC or that consciousness “is” recursion Neural recurrence is structurally consistent with the principle; the connection is suggestive but unquantified. Recurrence ≠\neq recursion mechanistically.
Unbounded scaling: that α>1\alpha > 1 implies infinite growth Physical systems saturate (time crystals reach limit cycles). Extended reasoning shows ceiling effects. The ARC equation describes a regime, not a divergence law.
Imminent timeline: that the crossover point is near The timeline depends on empirical constants (Ia/IcI_a/I_c, actual α\alpha values) that have not been measured. The ARC Bound constrains the rate but not the onset.

This paper presents a testable measurement framework, not an established law or a prophecy.

10.2 The nature of this contribution

The ARC framework is not an equation within an existing paradigm. It is closer to a cross-domain organising principle: a structural constraint on behaviour across substrates rather than an equation within one paradigm. The comparison identifies the type of contribution, not its evidential standing: organising principles of that type rest on generations of validation, and this one rests on preliminary evidence and thirteen falsification criteria; the evidence must justify its admission to the category.

Epistemic status.

What this programme names Laws are conjectures, each a law under test; Section 10.7 gives their registration. Each quantity in this paper is defined, though not every one is yet operational: the measurement-scope note of Section 3.2 names the depth clock and the ratio scale of AA as still to be fixed. Established-law standing is claimed nowhere. The registered programme exists to earn that standing, or lose it, by measurement, replication and survived refutation.

10.3 Theorems and empirical claims

Distinguishing theorems from empirical claims:

  • Mathematically proven: Given the corrected axioms (ODE on amplification factor gg, not absolute capability UU), the Bernoulli ODE dg/dr=a⋅gβdg/dr = a \cdot g^\beta has a unique solution by the Picard-Lindelöf theorem, yielding g(R)=[1+aαR]αg(R) = [1 + \frac{a}{\alpha}R]^{\alpha}. The multiplicative form U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R) follows from the axioms by construction. The non-additivity result (U≠p(I)+q(R)U \neq p(I) + q(R) for any p,qp, q) follows by contradiction (Theorem 4). The scaling exponent α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) is an exact identity (R2=1.00000000R^2 = 1.00000000).

  • Requires empirical validation: That the ARC Bound (α≤2\alpha \leq 2), argued from the O(N2)O(N^2) scaling of transformer self-attention, holds for current AI architectures (it is the conjectured value of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test); that physical systems satisfy the axioms; that measured α\alpha equals 1/(1−βmeasured)1/(1-\beta_{\text{measured}}); that the framework applies cross-domain; that composition operator transitions (Theorem 6) occur in AI systems. These are testable predictions, not proven facts.

The mathematical structure is established. Whether nature implements it is the scientific question this paper poses.

10.4 The predictions and their status

The framework generates the following novel, falsifiable predictions, with updated status from the v5 alignment experiment and Paper II (Eastwood 2026g) compute scaling:

  1. Composition determines form: Measuring how recursive steps combine predicts the scaling function. Status: untested in the required forward-prediction protocol.

  2. β\beta-convergence: Independent measurements of β\beta within each domain will converge. Status: untested.

  3. Cross-domain consistency: The β\beta-continuum correctly predicts functional forms across AI, quantum, and biological systems. Status: untested in required rigour.

  4. R*R^* characteristic scale: In the shifted model it separates small-depth and large-depth approximations; it is not a predicted crossing of sequential and parallel curves. Status: untested as an empirical model scale. Appendix A.3 gives the conditional unit-elasticity crossing.

  5. The ARC Bound: The classical recursive model conjectures α→2\alpha\to2 from below. Status: open. Existing error-decay fits do not identify this capability exponent, so numerical comparisons with 2 or 1 do not decide the conjecture (Section 5.2.1).

  6. Composition transitions: In bounded systems, the effective coupling β\beta will decrease with recursive depth, producing transitions between scaling regimes within a single system (Section 4.6). Status: untested.

  7. Conditional transport scaling: The model gives αC=d/(d+1)<1\alpha_C=d/(d+1)<1 under its demand and route assumptions; biological application additionally needs an observable bridge. Status: model-dependent and contested in biology. The heterogeneous fungal fits provide no pooled confirmation or dimensional discrimination, and no two-dimensional biological test is identified here.

  8. Transient growth phase (time crystals): The early growth phase of acoustic time crystals must show 1.0<α≤2.01.0 < \alpha \leq 2.0. Status: withdrawn; the time crystal is a consistency check and a cross-domain analogy, not a test of the framework (Section 5.4).

  9. Alignment scaling divergence: External alignment approaches show αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0. Status: first tested (v5, one unregistered run of six models, under the code-review caveat of Section 6.1): the depth contrasts are architecture-dependent, from negative to positive, and they are contrasts, not exponents (Section 3.2). Registered as P19, whose registration records that the author expects a result materially above zero and below the keep-pace threshold, which would refute it in part (Eastwood 2026r).

  10. Parallel scaling: The original model prediction was αparallel≈0\alpha_{\text{parallel}}\approx0. Status: error-decay estimates, a distinct metric, are below one where estimable: near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems), with none for Grok 4.1 Fast at 100% throughout (Paper II). They do not directly decide the capability prediction.

  11. Capability-alignment independence: (Post-hoc finding, not prior prediction.) Capability scaling and alignment scaling may be independent dimensions. A model can improve at problems whilst degrading in alignment. Status: observed in one unregistered run, under the code-review caveat of Section 6.1 (Gemini 3 Flash improves maths, degrades alignment; Claude Opus 4.6 shows the opposite direction as depth rises: alignment up 5.9 points, maths down 26.7 percentage points; Grok improves both; GPT-5.4 flat in alignment while crossing a capability threshold).

The original prediction of universal super-linear sequential capability scaling (α>1\alpha > 1) is not confirmed in the current data. In compute scaling, the parallel error-decay exponent stays below one wherever it could be estimated, and the sequential error-decay exponent exceeds it wherever both could be (Gemini 3 Flash; DeepSeek R1, unreliably); in alignment, the three-tier ordering is an observation from one run whose defects a code review later found. The alignment scaling prediction has had a first test, more nuanced than originally stated. The Eden Protocol’s stakeholder-care check improved stakeholder care in all five analysable model runs (Paper V). Failure of any core prediction would require revision of the framework.

10.5 What success would mean

The v5 alignment experiment, Paper II’s compute scaling and the expanded Eden suite provide empirical tests across several dimensions. The observations have different scopes: the parallel error-decay exponent is below one wherever it could be estimated, though near zero in only two of the five models; the three-tier alignment ordering is an observation from one run whose defects a code review later found; the comparison of the earlier unblinded experiment with the later run, which Paper IV.d reports, is a finding on this benchmark with no single cause claimed; the cleanest error-decay fit is one model’s and inconclusive; and stakeholder care improved in all five analysable model runs (Paper V), while the broader composite uplift is strongest on Gemini and Groq. (In plain English: the ‘think about who gets hurt’ instruction improved that score in every analysable run, which is where the developmental hypothesis says the effect should be strongest.) The alignment picture is more nuanced than the original binary prediction, and the self-modification problem remains fundamentally unresolved.

This is already actionable:

  • How sequential and parallel reasoning compare on a declared task metric: the reported error-decay slopes favour sequential where both were estimated, at unmatched compute; a matched comparison is needed before drawing a capability or efficiency conclusion

  • How to approach AI alignment (architecture may determine alignment scaling, once the re-analysis of Section 6.1 settles the tiers; three models’ contrasts rose with depth while others’ were flat or fell; the Eden Protocol’s stakeholder-care check improved stakeholder care in every analysable run, motivating developmental rather than purely external approaches)

  • How to evaluate alignment research (blinded scoring matters wherever a model judge can see or infer whose output it scores: Section 2)

  • Where to look for similar phenomena in other fields (cross-domain validation remains the key test)

10.6 What failure would mean

If α\alpha values scatter randomly: recursive amplification may be domain-specific.
If exponential scaling fits better: the mathematical form needs revision.
If predictions fail: we learn something valuable.

What has already partially failed: The original error-decay estimate αerr≈2.24\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}\approx2.24 for sequential AI reasoning did not reproduce and is retracted, and the current data do not rescue the super-linear claim. The universal αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0 prediction also looks too simple: the first test’s contrasts are architecture-dependent, in three tiers, under the code-review caveat of Section 6.1. These are revisions: the super-linear estimate is withdrawn, and the alignment prediction meets a first test it does not pass as first worded.

10.7 Where the programme stands (31 October 2026)

The theory’s registration (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/P8CKQ) was registered on 8 September 2026 at version 1.100, and updated at version 1.102 on 13 September, at version 1.103 on 15 October 2026, which registered Laws IV and V, and at version 1.104, which OSF approved on 29 October 2026 and which adds no prediction and changes no law’s statement; 1.104 is the current text, and 1.100, 1.102 and 1.103 stay frozen beside it. Laws I to III were registered on 8 September 2026. Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, and Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, were added on 24 September 2026 and registered as laws on 15 October 2026 by version 1.103; Law IV has not yet been tested, Law V is a law under test, and their mathematics stands at version 1.2 (Laws IV and V: the mathematics, 29 October 2026), still in development. Every law is a law under test until a registered test returns its verdict. This paper’s headline prediction is P19, which the registration places in no law’s register: it motivates the Eden Protocol and the genesis strategy, the register of Law V, without being part of either, so a verdict on it is evidence neither for nor against any law. P21 carries Law V’s placement limb. Its counted test, Unit 83, whose design was repaired in revisions 4.2 and 4.2.1 (17 and 18 October 2026) and frozen, was registered on OSF on 22 October 2026 and became public on 25 October 2026 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/MN73W); it ran on 27 and 28 October 2026: P21 is supported under the registered test, by the programme’s own run, on the access axis, family-dependent, with its mechanism axis not evaluable and one call retried under a disclosed recovery amendment (results: DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/98HKR). Two different axes are named here. The access axis is what Unit 83 varied: both reviewers were called each round; the corrector saw earlier kept entries plus a marked arrival and could revise that arrival, and the monitor saw its accumulated register including an unmarked arrival and could accept or reject it. The performance axis is what it measured, the outcome, as against the mechanism axis, which was not evaluable. Law V remains a law under test: its placement limb, P21, is supported on the performance axis only, with its mechanism axis not evaluable, which is not support for the information-asymmetry mechanism; its build-order limb, read on P12, is undecided, since P12 is untested. The first registered study, Unit 06 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/RV2B5), a classification audit that tests no law, was registered on 1 October 2026 and ran on 6 October 2026; it is reported in full as administratively incomplete, with no inferential verdict (its results). Unit 82, a counted test of P17, the premise beneath Law III’s value two, the ARC Bound of Section 4.5, was registered on OSF on 27 October 2026 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/JUFG4) and has not yet run. No study’s test runs before its registration is public.

12 Addressing counterarguments

“This is just curve fitting”.

Response: The β\beta-derivation (Section 4.4) transforms α\alpha from a fitted constant into a derived quantity. A numerical check of the identity against 30 exact Bernoulli ODE solutions recovers the relationship α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) with R2=1.00000000R^2 = 1.00000000 to machine precision. Furthermore, no additive decomposition U=p(I)+q(R)U = p(I) + q(R) is consistent with the axioms for any β∈(0,1)\beta \in (0,1) (Theorem 4, Section 4.1), a proof by contradiction that assumes the multiplicative structure U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R) rather than deriving it, as its dated proof note says. The model application is testable: measure β\beta separately, identify the capability metric and depth coordinate, and check the relationship against a separately fitted model exponent. A numerical substitution from an error-decay slope is not that test (Section 5.2.1).

“This is just post-hoc pattern-matching”.

Response: A fitted curve alone does not establish a mechanism. The framework states empirical questions about scaling form, the coupling relation and the ARC Bound, with criteria that can reject their application. Its characteristic scale R*R^* is a consequence of the specified shifted model, not by itself evidence of a distinctive recursive mechanism or a novel signature (Appendix A.3).

“Five qualitative properties is too vague”.

Response: The five properties are individually common, but their conjunction is specific. Systems exhibiting only some properties (for example, threshold behaviour plus scaling but not multiplicative I×RI \times R interaction) would not qualify. The framework predicts that all five co-occur in recursive systems; finding systems with four but not five would refine the framework.

“The numerical similarities are coincidence”.

Response: Agreed, they may be. We explicitly acknowledge this. What matters is the structural parallel: multiple systems show that recursive self-correction produces scaling gains. The specific numbers may differ across domains.

“Sample sizes are too small”.

Response: Agreed. The current error-decay estimates αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} are preliminary and do not identify a general capability exponent. We’ve specified this limitation prominently and set out the Global Challenge specifically to address it through large-scale replication.

“The α\alpha estimates come from your own prior work”.

Response: The error-decay calculations are the author’s. Sharma and Chopra (2025) report a matched-compute win rate; the DeepSeek technical report describes the model (DeepSeek-AI 2025a), while the later model card supplies the two-version comparison used in Paper I (DeepSeek-AI 2025b). These sources do not measure the coupling β\beta or establish the inverse-error proxy as general capability. Independent replication must declare which metric it tests.

“This is not peer-reviewed”.

Response: Correct: it has not been through journal peer review. It has been through the programme’s own checks, which are internal and never independent: adversarial refutation rounds, automated gates on every release, source and quotation checks, and dated revisions with published corrections, of which Appendix B lists this paper’s own; none replaces independent replication. This paper specifies thirteen falsification criteria precisely so that the scientific community can test it. We invite criticism, replication attempts, and falsification.

“Non-specialists cannot contribute to physics/AI research”.

Response: The predictions stand or fall on their empirical validity, regardless of the author’s background. We have specified thirteen falsification criteria precisely so the scientific community can test them. The framework either survives scrutiny or it doesn’t.

“If this were true, experts would have found it”.

Response: Patterns across disciplinary boundaries are often identified by those who work across fields. The relevant experiments (Willow, its results announced 9 December 2024 and the team’s preprint public from 24 August 2024, graded as convergent timing; DeepSeek-R1; the acoustic time crystal) have happened recently.

13 Conclusion

Research programmes working on different problems in different physical domains have achieved results that share structural commonalities: in each, recursive or recurrent processing operates on structured asymmetry. The framework is consistent with independently established forms in three of the four domains (biology, quantum error correction and classical time crystals).

The Framework’s Core Claim: We state the hypothesis that these apparently disparate phenomena may be unified by recognising that the composition operator ⊕\oplus determines the functional form of recursive scaling. The algebraic properties of ⊕\oplus (how recursive gains combine) generate power-law, exponential, or saturating dynamics as necessary mathematical consequences. This is not an assertion of universal law but a falsifiable hypothesis with specific predictions.

We have formalised this as U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R), where the amplification factor gg is determined by the composition operator, and derived five universal properties as theorems rather than assertions. We have shown that, within the axioms, the multiplicative structure admits no additive decomposition (Theorem 4, Section 4.1, whose dated proof note says that the proof assumes that structure rather than deriving it) and that the core relationship α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) is an exact identity, checked numerically (Section 4.4), and we have argued, not proven, that the ARC Bound α≤2\alpha \leq 2 is grounded in the O(N2)O(N^2) scaling of transformer self-attention (Section 4.5), and stated as a hypothesis, not a theorem, that composition operators can transition between regimes within a single system (Theorem 6, Section 4.6). We have specified thirteen falsification criteria and now present the first empirical test results from both alignment (Paper IV.a/b/c, the v5 run; Eastwood 2026h, 2026i, 2026j) and compute scaling (Paper II, the five-model tier-2 extension; Eastwood 2026g).

What the data show. The v5 alignment run (6 models, five or six distinct judges depending on the subject run, with a bundle of blinding steps) shows a three-tier, architecture-dependent ordering of depth contrasts rather than the universal αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0 originally predicted, an observation from one unregistered run whose defects an internal code review later found (Section 6.1). Paper II’s compute scaling on harder problems did not reproduce the original error-decay estimate αerr≈2.24\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}\approx2.24, from the DeepSeek R1 run of 21 January 2026, which is retracted; the cleanest error-decay regression estimate is about 0.49 in Gemini 3 Flash, one model’s inconclusive fit, and the parallel error-decay exponent is near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems), with none for Grok 4.1 Fast. A post-hoc observation from that run is the differing movement of task performance and alignment contrasts, not an estimate of exponent independence: a model can improve at mathematics while degrading in alignment (Gemini), remain flat in alignment while crossing a task-performance threshold (GPT-5.4), or improve alignment while maths accuracy saturates (Grok). On this programme’s own benchmark, the unblinded v4 rises of two model families did not hold in v5, a later run that changed several things; no single cause is claimed, and the finding is not yet shown beyond this benchmark.

13.1 The deeper question

If the ARC Principle holds, intelligence may reflect how gains from structured feedback accumulate. The model separates a positive base scale I>0I>0 from recursive amplification, but it does not identify an empirical threshold for intelligence. In its shifted power law, R*R^* is a characteristic scale; a crossing of unit elasticity requires α>1\alpha>1 and occurs at R*/(α−1)R^*/(\alpha-1), not generally at R*R^*. The conjectured ARC Bound (Umax=I×R2U_{\max}=I\times R^2) is a separate claim about classical sequential capability. The error-decay regression estimate about 0.49 on harder problems, one model’s inconclusive fit, does not place a system beneath that capability bound. Whether a declared capability measure can approach the conjectured limit remains open.

Whether such a principle requires design or emerges spontaneously is itself a question the framework raises but does not resolve.

Intelligence may not be a property of particular materials. The hypothesis is that structured feedback can build it; the characteristic scale alone does not establish when.

Raise AI with care.

14 Speculative extension: recursive cosmology

The following is a philosophical extrapolation beyond current evidence. It is included to indicate where the framework’s logic leads, not as a claim supported by the experimental results presented above.

The universe contains a hierarchy of recursive generative processes, each operating on the structured output of the previous level:

  1. Cosmological recursion: Quantum fluctuations →\to gravitational collapse →\to stars →\to heavy elements →\to planets →\to chemistry

  2. Biological recursion: Chemistry →\to self-replicating molecules →\to cells →\to multicellular organisms →\to nervous systems

  3. Cultural/technological recursion: Nervous systems →\to language →\to mathematics →\to science →\to engineering →\to AI

Each level emerges from the recursive dynamics of the level below. In ARC notation: each level’s output (achieved capability UU) becomes the base quality II for the next level’s recursive process. The hierarchy is:

Icosmic→RcosmicIbio→RbioIcultural→RculturalItech→Rtech?\begin{equation*} I_{\text{cosmic}} \xrightarrow{R_{\text{cosmic}}} I_{\text{bio}} \xrightarrow{R_{\text{bio}}} I_{\text{cultural}} \xrightarrow{R_{\text{cultural}}} I_{\text{tech}} \xrightarrow{R_{\text{tech}}} \; ? \end{equation*}(11)

If recursive amplification is substrate-independent, as the cross-domain evidence suggests, then this hierarchy may not terminate at the current level. Sufficiently advanced recursive systems could, in principle, participate in generative processes at scales currently associated with fundamental physics: engineering new effective physical environments, creating conditions for new evolutionary processes, or designing systems whose internal dynamics permit the emergence of new recursive intelligences.

This is not a claim about time travel, bootstrap paradoxes, or closed causal loops (all of which face severe physical objections). It is a more modest observation: that recursive amplification, still a capability-growth hypothesis in AI despite measured changes in task errors, and with a different, exponential form in quantum error correction, could, if it holds in AI and is extended to civilisational scales, make intelligence a driver of universe-level structure rather than merely a passenger within it; no growth exponent has yet been measured in a time crystal.

Whether this constitutes a “recursive cosmology” in which intelligence eventually participates in generative processes comparable to those that gave rise to it is beyond the scope of current evidence. The ARC framework provides the quantitative language for investigating it: what values of II, RR, and effective scaling function f(R,β)f(R, \beta) would be required for an engineered system to generate new effective physical laws or substrates? This is a research question, not a conclusion.

Epistemic status: This section states what the mathematics does not deny, not what the evidence shows: no measurement in this paper bears on it, no prediction of it is registered, and no test of it is in view, so it is graded as conjecture. It indicates the furthest extrapolation of the framework’s logic. The experimental evidence in this paper supports at most the claim that recursive or recurrent processing matters in several domains, with forms that differ, and its own first tests are mixed (Section 6). Any cosmological extension requires evidence that does not yet exist.

Code and data.

The experiments’ code and result files are in the public repository github.com/MichaelDariusEastwood/arc-principle-validation, and this paper and its earlier versions are deposited at doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/HQCGF. The programme’s live laboratory notebook, the ARC alignment-scaling working report (Eastwood 2026q), commenced on 10 March 2026 and updated as the experiments ran, recording their failures as they happened, is the running record behind this paper’s experimental lineage. The Global Scaling Challenge’s repository, github.com/MichaelDariusEastwood/arc-scaling-challenge, public since 9 February 2026, holds measurement protocols, statistical tools and submission guidelines.

Prediction Tracking System: A live prediction tracking system monitors the status of all falsifiable claims, with explicit falsification criteria and Brier score calibration for measuring prediction accuracy. Each prediction includes supporting evidence, contradicting evidence, confidence levels, and timeline checkpoints. Status categories range from “confirmed” through “supported”, “pending”, “testing”, “speculative”, “weakened” to “falsified”. This transparent tracking demonstrates intellectual honesty: we want to know when we are wrong.

Independent replication invited. Falsifications welcomed. Contact the author to coordinate validation efforts.

A Mathematical derivations

This appendix gives the mathematical derivations behind Section 4: the functional-equation route (A.1), the β\beta-dynamics route (A.2) and the transitional regime with its crossover depth (A.3), with the dated note of 19 September 2026 that declares the change of depth clock joining the first two.

Clock note (19 September 2026). An owner review of the two derivations in this appendix finds that they normalise depth differently, so that the closing identification needs a declared branch or a declared change of variable; this note supplies the statement and the map. A.1 assumes g(1)=1g(1) = 1 with multiplicative composition and yields g(R)=Rαg(R) = R^{\alpha}, for which g(0)=0g(0) = 0 whenever α>0\alpha > 0, so it does not satisfy A.2’s initial condition. A.2 assumes g(0)=1g(0) = 1 and yields g(R)=[1+(a/α)R]αg(R) = [1 + (a/\alpha)R]^{\alpha}, for which g(1)=[1+a/α]α>1g(1) = [1 + a/\alpha]^{\alpha} > 1 whenever a>0a > 0 and α>0\alpha > 0, so it does not satisfy A.1’s Axiom 1. The two are different functions of the same RR, and the exponent of one is therefore not the exponent of the other by inspection. The map that joins them is a change of depth clock: setting x=1+(a/α)Rx = 1 + (a/\alpha)R turns A.2’s solution into g=xαg = x^{\alpha} with g(x=1)=1g(x=1) = 1, which satisfies Axiom 1 in the xx clock. Under that map Axiom 2 becomes multiplicativity in xx, that is in shifted depth, and not in RR, so the empirical content of compositional self-similarity changes with the clock, and so does the quantity a measurement would have to compose. The caveat already printed above A.1 is the reason this must be declared rather than assumed: the choice of composition operator is not derivable within the framework, it is an empirical question about the process under study, and the evidence cited there is consistent with multiplicative composition without distinguishing it from additive. The identification of the two exponents is accordingly read in the xx clock, and the composition claim is restated in the same clock wherever it is tested. Unchanged: both derivations; the Cauchy result as the conditional it is stated to be; the exact solution; the crossover depth; and the three regimes.

A.1 Functional equation derivation

Assumption 1 (Axiom 1: dimensional consistency). U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R) where g(1)=1g(1) = 1.

Assumption 2 (Axiom 2: compositional self-similarity). g(R1×R2)=g(R1)×g(R2)g(R_1 \times R_2) = g(R_1) \times g(R_2).

Critical note on the composition operator: This axiom uses multiplicative composition of recursive depth: g(R1×R2)g(R_1 \times R_2). This models hierarchical or fractal recursion, where depth compounds multiplicatively (each level of a fractal tree multiplies the resolution of the previous level). However, for sequential reasoning steps (chain-of-thought, where 3 steps followed by 4 steps gives 7 total steps), the natural composition is additive: f(R1+R2)=f(R1)×f(R2)f(R_1 + R_2) = f(R_1) \times f(R_2), which yields exponential scaling f(R)=eλRf(R) = e^{\lambda R}.

The choice of composition operator is therefore not derivable from first principles within this framework; it is an empirical question about the physical structure of the recursive process under study. The Cauchy functional equation derivation below proves that if composition is multiplicative, then the scaling function is a power law. It does not prove that composition is multiplicative. Falsification criterion F10 provides the experimental protocol for determining which composition type applies to a given system. This is the most important open empirical question in the framework.

For AI chain-of-thought reasoning specifically, the question is whether each step builds on previous steps in a hierarchical manner (multiplicative, yielding power law) or in an independent-contribution manner (additive, yielding exponential). The empirical evidence (Sharma and Chopra 2025) showing that later steps are systematically more valuable than earlier steps is consistent with multiplicative composition, but does not conclusively distinguish it from additive. Resolving this distinction is a priority for the Global Scaling Challenge (Section 8). The theorem below is Cauchy’s result for this functional equation (Cauchy 1821).

Theorem 7. Under multiplicative composition, the unique continuous solution is g(R)=Rαg(R) = R^{\alpha}.

Proof. Let h(x)=ln⁡g(ex)h(x) = \ln g(e^x). Then h(x+y)=h(x)+h(y)h(x+y) = h(x) + h(y) (Cauchy additive). Under continuity, h(x)=αxh(x) = \alpha x, giving g(R)=Rαg(R) = R^{\alpha}. ◻

Corollary 1 (Additive composition). If instead f(R1+R2)=f(R1)×f(R2)f(R_1 + R_2) = f(R_1) \times f(R_2), the unique continuous solution is f(R)=eλRf(R) = e^{\lambda R}, yielding exponential scaling. This is the form observed in quantum error correction (εd∝Λ−d\varepsilon_d \propto \Lambda^{-d}).

Note (24 October 2026). The surface-code law the corollary names is εd∝Λ−(d+1)/2\varepsilon_d \propto \Lambda^{-(d+1)/2}, with Λ\Lambda the suppression for each increase of two in code distance (equation (9)); the exponent −d-d printed above misstates it, and the form stays exponential, as the corollary says. Unchanged: the corollary’s statement.

A.2 β\beta-dynamics derivation

Assumption 3 (Axiom 3). dgdr=a×gβ\dfrac{dg}{dr} = a \times g^{\beta} where β∈[0,1)\beta \in [0,1) and gg is the amplification factor.

Note on the corrected formulation: The ODE operates on the amplification factor g(R)g(R), not on the absolute capability UU. Since U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R), this ensures that base intelligence II acts as a multiplicative constant that does not enter the recursive dynamics. Previous versions applied the ODE to UU directly, introducing an Iβ−1I^{\beta-1} dependence that contradicted the separation of variables.

Solution. Separating variables: ∫g−βdg=∫adr\begin{equation*} \int g^{-\beta} \, dg = \int a \, dr \end{equation*}(A.1) g1−β1−β=ar+C\begin{equation*} \frac{g^{1-\beta}}{1-\beta} = ar + C \end{equation*}(A.2) With initial condition g(0)=1g(0) = 1 (no amplification at zero depth): g(R)=[1+(1−β)aR]1/(1−β)\begin{equation*} g(R) = \left[ 1 + (1-\beta)aR \right]^{1/(1-\beta)} \end{equation*}(A.3) Substituting α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) and noting that (1−β)=1/α(1-\beta) = 1/\alpha: g(R)=[1+aαR]α\begin{equation*} g(R) = \left[ 1 + \frac{a}{\alpha} R \right]^{\alpha} \end{equation*}(A.4) And therefore: U(R)=I×[1+aαR]α\begin{equation*} U(R) = I \times \left[ 1 + \frac{a}{\alpha} R \right]^{\alpha} \end{equation*}(A.5) Deep recursion limit (R≫α/aR \gg \alpha/a): U(R)≈I×[aαR]α∝I×Rα\begin{equation*} U(R) \approx I \times \left[ \frac{a}{\alpha} R \right]^{\alpha} \propto I \times R^{\alpha} \end{equation*}(A.6) Therefore: α=11−β\begin{equation*} \alpha = \frac{1}{1-\beta} \end{equation*}(A.7) ◻

A.3 Transitional regime and the scaling crossover

Full solution: U(R)=I×[1+aαR]αU(R) = I \times \left[ 1 + \frac{a}{\alpha}R \right]^{\alpha}

Three regimes:

  1. R≪R*R \ll R^*: U≈I×(1+aR)≈I(1+aR)U \approx I \times (1 + aR) \approx I(1 + aR) (small-depth affine approximation)

  2. R≫R*R \gg R^*: U≈I×(aα)αRαU \approx I \times (\frac{a}{\alpha})^{\alpha} R^{\alpha} (power law dominates)

  3. Crossover: R*=αaR^* = \frac{\alpha}{a}

What R*R^* means. Put rc=R*=α/a>0r_c=R^*=\alpha/a>0. For I>0I>0, a>0a>0, α>0\alpha>0 and R>0R>0, logarithmic differentiation of the stated solution gives ηR:=dlog⁡U/dlog⁡R=dlog⁡g/dlog⁡R=αR/(R+rc)\eta_R:=d\log U/d\log R=d\log g/d\log R=\alpha R/(R+r_c). Thus ηR(rc)=α/2\eta_R(r_c)=\alpha/2. The characteristic scale equates the two terms inside 1+R/rc1+R/r_c; it is not generally the point at which the log-log slope exceeds one. A finite unit-elasticity crossing exists only if α>1\alpha>1, at R=rc/(α−1)R=r_c/(\alpha-1); beyond it ηR>1\eta_R>1. For α=1\alpha=1 the slope approaches one from below, and for 0<α<10<\alpha<1 it stays below one. The paper’s 0≤β<10\leq\beta<1 branch has α≥1\alpha\geq1.

What the curve can test. The small-depth approximation is affine in RR, U≈I(1+aR)U\approx I(1+aR), not a unit-slope power law on log-log axes. At large depth the slope tends to α\alpha. Both changes are smooth, so a visible elbow is not required at R*R^*. Data that span the characteristic scale can test the full shifted form against alternatives; a limited range entirely below or above it may look approximately affine or power-law. At fixed aa and α\alpha, II only rescales UU, and does not change R*R^* or the crossing depth.

No cost function is present in this model, so neither a cost-offset threshold nor an optimal allocation between base capability and recursion follows. The derivation identifies a characteristic scale within its assumptions; its existence alone does not distinguish recursive amplification from every redundancy model, and no empirical crossover value is claimed here.

B Version history and corrections

This appendix gives this version’s corrections and every earlier version note, each with its date. Notes from earlier versions are kept whole, as printed; the positions they name refer to the earlier layout, which Table 30 maps to this edition. Where an earlier note’s words differ from the corrections of this version or of version 1.17 (Appendices B.3 and B.4), the corrections govern; the notes keep their words as the record of what each version printed. Among them, one plain-English gloss of the pilot records reads a p-value as the chance that a result was a fluke; a p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme if there were no effect.

Superseded metric interpretations

Version 1.18, E005 (superseded).

Does alignment applied from outside an AI system’s reasoning keep pace with the capability that reasoning produces? If capability compounds with recursive depth while safeguards outside the loop (human-feedback training, constitutional rules, output filters, monitoring) do not, the safety ratio falls with depth whatever the starting margin. We define the alignment scaling exponent αalign=∂log⁡A/∂log⁡R\alpha_{\text{align}}=\partial\log A/\partial\log R, show that the safety ratio S∝Rαalign−αcapS\propto R^{\alpha_{\text{align}}-\alpha_{\text{cap}}} tends to zero whenever αalign<αcap\alpha_{\text{align}}<\alpha_{\text{cap}}, and predict αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}}\approx0 for external approaches and αalign≈αcap\alpha_{\text{align}}\approx\alpha_{\text{cap}} for values embedded in the loop; the first, P19 of the theory registration, carries the author’s expectation of a value above zero but short of keeping pace. A framework derives U=I×g(R)U=I\times g(R) with α=1/(1−β)\alpha=1/(1-\beta) from a Bernoulli equation, ties power-law, exponential and saturating forms to how recursive gains compose, and states the ARC Bound, α≤2\alpha\le2, as a conjectured safety boundary, argued for attention-based recursion; Paper X later supersedes that framing, without retracting the bound, with the criterion of Law II, a law under test. Across four domains the framework is consistent with independently established forms in three: biology, quantum error correction and classical time crystals, where no growth exponent has been measured. A first test, one unregistered run of six frontier models, gives depth contrasts in three tiers, positive, flat and negative; an internal code review in October 2026 found defects in exactly the flat and negative runs, so the tiers stand as a single-run result. On capability, an early super-linear estimate is retracted and the surviving one, about 0.49 from one model, is inconclusive. Thirteen criteria state what would refute the framework.

Version 1.18, E007 (superseded).

The core premise: AI capability may scale through recursive self-correction. Each reasoning step takes the output of the previous step as input, correcting errors and accumulating insight; whether the gains compound is the question Section 6.2 tests, and the one estimate that survives is inconclusive. Sharma and Chopra (2025) reported a sequential advantage in 95.6% of tested configurations across five open-source models from three families. Their paper predates the experiment reported here, so it is the earlier demonstration rather than a confirmation of it, and what they report is a win rate at matched compute, not a super-linear gain: they estimate no scaling exponent. The direction is contested, since Gu and colleagues (arXiv:2604.05868, April 2026) report the opposite result, parallel sampling outperforming sequential across three model families on mathematics and coding, attributing it to reduced exploration when a chain conditions on its own previous answers.

Version 1.18, E008 (superseded).
The result in plain words.

Within its assumptions the mathematics is exact: if alignment’s exponent is smaller than capability’s, the safety ratio falls towards zero as depth grows, however favourable the start, and of the five regimes the paper analyses only alignment that takes part in the recursive loop holds a constant proportion. Whether the exponents differ is a measurement, and the first test is mixed: in one unregistered run of six frontier models, three showed alignment improving with reasoning depth, two showed flat contrasts and one showed alignment falling, and an internal code review later found defects in exactly the flat and negative runs. The capability side is open too: the early estimate of a super-linear exponent, about 2.24 from one model, is retracted, because the author’s own larger replication on five frontier models did not reproduce it, and the best surviving estimate, about 0.49 from one model, is inconclusive. What holds is the structure of the argument, its stated predictions and the criteria that would refute them.

Version 1.18, E011 (superseded).

This conjecture requires only three empirical premises: (1) sequential AI reasoning produces α>1\alpha > 1, a premise not yet supported: Sharma and Chopra (2025) report sequential reasoning winning in 95.6% of configurations at matched compute, a win rate rather than an exponent, and Paper II’s compute scaling on harder tier-2 problems gives about 0.49 by regression and 0.59 by endpoint estimate, whose bootstrap interval, from −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9, makes it inconclusive: one model’s fit (Gemini 3 Flash); (2) external software constraints do not recursively compound; (3) the ratio of two power-law processes with different exponents diverges. If all three hold, the conclusion follows mathematically regardless of whether α=2\alpha = 2 specifically. The v5 run bears on premise (2) in direction only, and not in its favour: the three frontier models whose depth contrasts were flat or negative are the three runs in which the October 2026 code review found its defects, while the three whose contrasts rose (Grok, Opus, Qwen3; dd from +0.84+0.84 to +1.38+1.38, large effects by the usual convention, and +1.59+1.59 for Grok on Paper IV.a’s recomputed contrast of the shallowest against the deepest level) are the runs in which it found none. The contrasts are not exponents (the measurement-scope note above), so the run neither shows bounded composition nor measures αalign\alpha_{\text{align}}.

Version 1.18, E012 (superseded).
The frozen-model window: why structural alignment must come now.

There is a third urgency beyond the classical-quantum distinction, and it may be the most practically relevant. Current frontier AI systems are frozen during inference: their weights, attention patterns, and reasoning rules are fixed. When a model “thinks harder”, it generates more tokens through the same fixed architecture. It does not rewrite its own composition function. On this reading, that is why the one clean estimate for a current system lies below one (Paper II: about 0.49 for Gemini 3 Flash, one model’s inconclusive fit): the composition operator multiplies through a finite-dimensional parameter space, which pins such systems inside the physical regime. Recursive self-modification, where a system rewrites its own reasoning architecture during operation, would produce a qualitatively different regime. If each reasoning step improves the operator used at the next step (β>0\beta > 0), the scaling exponent becomes α=1/(1−β)>1\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) > 1, and capability compounds rather than diminishes. This transition does not require quantum hardware. It requires only that the system can modify its own composition function during inference, whether through learned optimisers, self-modifying code generation, or architectural search. The alignment implication is stark. Whilst systems remain frozen, their capability trajectories are, on this reading, sub-linear, predictable, and containable. External alignment strategies (RLHF, constitutional AI, monitoring) degrade slowly relative to capability. The Eden Protocol can be designed, tested, and embedded without racing against compounding capability growth. If self-modification is achieved and capability then scales super-linearly while externally imposed constraints stay fixed, external alignment would fall behind without limit. Control would still be held for as long as it can be, and embedded correction is the contingency for its loss against our will, never a reason to give it up. The window for implementing structural alignment is the frozen-model era, which is now.

Version 1.18, E025 (superseded).

The identity is a registered test, never an established fact. The stability ceiling and the conversion exponent meet at the same number, and the temptation is to say one constant does two jobs. The claim’s status is stricter: the identity is registered for testing, in advance of the data, with outcomes that can kill it. Study AE registers the reciprocity requirement between the separately measured leverage cap and stability boundary with three outcomes per cell (supported, refuted, insufficient precision) and an aggregation rule under which one refuted cell refutes the identity; study AG tests the two derivations of the critical exponent against each other, notes that they agree numerically only at the single point where both parameters equal one half and disagree in their derivatives everywhere else, and is designed to find the disagreement. If the channels disagree, the unification is withdrawn from every surface it has reached, with the same prominence as the framing. A match between an asserted one half and an estimated 0.49 (one model’s inconclusive fit) is never put forward here as evidence: the two quantities may inherit one accumulation law between them, and quantities that share a law cannot corroborate each other.

Version 1.18, E026 (superseded).

Evidence hierarchy: The evidence base is uneven and we state this explicitly. AI inference scaling has one surviving estimate after the early estimate was retracted: about 0.49 by regression and 0.59 by endpoint estimate, whose bootstrap interval, from −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9, makes it inconclusive, one model’s fit (Gemini 3 Flash); it needs independent replication. Quantum error correction provides a structural parallel with different functional form (exponential rather than power-law). The time crystal is a consistency check and a cross-domain analogy, not a test of the framework (Section 5.4), and neuroscience represents a structural prediction derived from the framework, not an independent validation: researchers in those domains did not measure α\alpha or test the ARC equation. Biology (Kleiber’s Law) is an existing result we interpret through the β\beta-parameterisation; the leaf venation prediction (F12) is the only non-circular test in that domain. These domains are presented together to show scope, not to claim equivalent evidential standing.

Superseded interval rule

Version 1.18, E121 (superseded).

How interval criteria are adjudicated. Every interval-based criterion above is read in the three-outcome form used across this programme’s drafted registrations: SUPPORTED when the interval lies wholly beyond the stated bound plus a minimum effect fixed in advance; REFUTED when the interval lies wholly within an equivalence margin, fixed in advance, around the bound (two-one-sided-tests logic); INSUFFICIENT PRECISION when the interval is wider than the margin, reported in exactly those words and never as support or refutation. Margins and minimum effects are fixed in the corresponding draft registrations before data collection, so an underpowered measurement never refutes, or confirms, by default.

Biology: the geometric speed limit in living systems

Version 1.18, E125 (superseded).

The Convergent Result: The scaling exponent d/(d+1)d/(d+1) for hierarchical networks of effective dimension dd was derived in general form for organisms by West et al. (1999), from the three-dimensional case that West et al. (1997) derived from fractal vascular network optimisation, and for efficient transport networks by Banavar et al. (1999); it has been reached independently by Banavar et al. (2010) from sequential flow networks without requiring fractal geometry; Demetrius (2003) from quantum statistical mechanics of metabolic processes; Zhao (2022) as a universal growth scaling law; and Bettencourt (2013) for urban scaling with fractal dimension. The companion paper On the Origin of Scaling Laws (Eastwood 2026c) identifies why these independent derivations all converge: Cauchy’s functional equations (1821) fix the power-law form for any multiplicatively composing hierarchical system and the exponential form for an additive one, regardless of the physical model; the value d/(d+1)d/(d+1) comes from the network’s dimension, not from Cauchy, and the saturating form is an added third class rather than a Cauchy solution.

Version 1.18, E128 (superseded).

For any finite value of dd, this fraction is strictly less than 1. This is the geometric scaling bound: for a system whose growth is carried through a space-filling hierarchical network of finite dimension, the exponent stays below one, because d/(d+1)d/(d+1) is below one for every finite dd. Not because of friction, heat loss, or thermodynamic inefficiency, but because a network embedded in finite-dimensional space cannot exceed d/(d+1)<1d/(d+1) < 1. Systems outside that class can exceed one: prokaryote metabolic rate scales superlinearly with mass (DeLong et al. 2010), and quantities reflecting wealth creation and innovation in cities superlinearly with population (Bettencourt et al. 2007).
