The unifying insight is dimensional generality. Three predicted numbers, one half, two thirds and three quarters, from one equation with zero free parameters; the first and last have been set against published measurements, and the second awaits its test in leaf venation (F12), no valid two-dimensional animal test having been identified. West et al. (1997) derived the 34\tfrac{3}{4} exponent from a detailed model of three-dimensional fractal vascular networks, a landmark result. But their model as originally stated predicts only 34\tfrac{3}{4}. The surface area hypothesis predicts 23\tfrac{2}{3} but not 34\tfrac{3}{4} or 12\tfrac{1}{2}. The general d/(d+1)d/(d+1) formula, stated by West et al. (1999) and Banavar et al. (1999) and developed in later work (Banavar et al. 2010; Zhao 2022), predicts all three from a single equation with one parameter: the dimension of the internal transport network. The ARC Principle’s contribution is showing, via Cauchy’s functional equations, that the three-form constraint (power law, exponential, saturating) explains why all independent derivations arrive at the same result.

Version 1.18, E135 (superseded).
Why ‘thermodynamic drag’ was wrong.
Version 1.18, E136 (superseded).

Previous versions of this paper explained biological sub-linear scaling through ‘thermodynamic drag’, the physical costs of pumping fluids, dissipating heat, and distributing resources. This explanation was correct in observational detail but fundamentally misleading about mechanism. The reason network-supplied systems scale sub-linearly is not energetic cost. It is geometric necessity: d/(d+1)<1d/(d+1) < 1 for all finite dd. You cannot make a three-dimensional body have a four-dimensional vascular network. The constraint is the shape of space, not the price of pumping blood.

Version 1.18, E137 (superseded).

The critical safety insight. Living systems whose growth runs through supply networks have been held below the geometric scaling bound, the d/(d+1)d/(d+1) relation derived in general form by West et al. (1999), from the three-dimensional case of West et al. (1997), and by Banavar et al. (1999), and reached independently by Banavar et al. (2010), Demetrius (2003), Zhao (2022) and Bettencourt (2013); prokaryotes, whose metabolism is not limited by such a network, scale superlinearly (DeLong et al. 2010). The computation a brain or a machine performs is physical too, and obeys every physical bound. What differs is the variable. The bound d/(d+1)d/(d+1) concerns how metabolic rate grows with the mass of a body supplied through a space-filling network; the ARC Principle concerns how capability grows with recursive depth, which this framework writes as α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta), above one for any positive self-referential coupling. Nothing in the geometry of the network fixes that second exponent, which is why it has to be measured, and why a value above one would contradict no physical law. If it exceeds one, the bound that held network-limited growth gives no comfort for recursive intelligence; that is why AI safety is, on this framework, a question about an exponent and not a policy preference.

The ARC Bound (a novel prediction). For recursive intelligence, the scaling exponent is bounded by α≤2\alpha \leq 2 (equivalently, β≤0.5\beta \leq 0.5). For attention-based architectures, the O(N2)O(N^2) scaling of self-attention provides the concrete computational basis: each reasoning step can cross-reference at most NN previous steps, producing at most quadratic information density. Version 1.18, E147 (superseded).

A ceiling on a class of mechanism: The ARC Bound is a mechanism-class ceiling of the kind thermodynamics made familiar. Just as a heat engine’s maximum efficiency is fixed by its operating temperatures regardless of engineering, on this argument no attention-based sequential recursive system would exceed α=2\alpha = 2, because transformer self-attention scales as O(N2)O(N^2). The analogy holds in the part that matters: a mechanism-class ceiling binds its class, and a device built on a different mechanism is not bound by it at all. Both are ceilings on a class of mechanism, not statements about what is physically possible. Individual systems may fall short due to imperfect coupling, noise, or architectural constraints (and physically embedded systems face the stricter geometric scaling bound of Section 5.6), but the ceiling for classical sequential computation is fixed by the quadratic geometry of cross-referencing. A system driven above that ceiling does not stay coherent there, so a durably stable measurement above α=2\alpha = 2 would refute the bound under F5, while an unstable excursion would be consistent with it; F11, the earlier criterion, refutes on a sustained magnitude alone. A ceiling of this kind tells us when to stop optimising within a paradigm and when a fundamentally different approach (e.g., additive composition, quantum coherence) is required to exceed it.

B.3 Version 1.18

Paper III v1.18, 31 October 2026.

This version brings the paper’s status to its date: the result of Unit 83, the grading of the acoustic time crystal, the versions of the works it cites, and the corrections that bear on its text. No theorem, equation, derivation or measured value changes, and no date of any claim moves.

Corrections in this version.

Each was checked at its source, and each is made wherever the corrected wording stood.

  • Unit 83. Its results were made public on 29 October 2026 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/98HKR), and the results package is now among the references. Section 10.7 now states its result for P21 in the form its registration requires, with the results DOI, and what the result means for Law V under the registration’s verdict rule: its placement limb is supported on the performance axis only, and its build-order limb is undecided. The first-page footnote gives Law V as a law under test, and Appendix E and Table 34 refer to Section 10.7. In each of these places version 1.17 said that the report of the run was not yet public.

  • The acoustic time crystal. The earlier prediction for it, a power law with an exponent above one, is withdrawn: the framework’s composition rule gives the same onset form as the established account of the instability, so the time crystal is a consistency check and a cross-domain analogy, not a test of the framework, and no study of it is registered; Unit 20 (study-t) is kept as a consistency check, not as a registration. Version 1.17 called onset recordings the deciding data, and that study the deciding instrument for the oscillation’s growth from rest and a draft registration still to be submitted. Section 5.4 now states the grading once, and the transient-phase protocol, the physical prediction and the three falsification conditions it printed as current are kept whole in Appendix B.8; its Caveat no longer says that plotting oscillation amplitude against cycle number and fitting power-law against linear models would directly test whether α>1\alpha > 1 in this domain. Criterion F9 stays, as this paper’s own criterion, graded so, with its rival account beside it, where version 1.17 printed it as “Time crystal shows α>1\alpha > 1”, tested by measuring stability against depth and falsified by α≤1\alpha \leq 1 in a time crystal. The prediction for the growth phase in Section 10.4 and its row in Table 22 are marked withdrawn, where they read untested, and Table 27 gives the grading, where it set the measurement out as an experimental priority. Section 8 no longer offers the time crystal for direct tests of α\alpha, Section 5 no longer calls it a structural prediction derived from the framework, and Section 4.3 no longer calls the Constraint Principle independently testable through criterion F3, which already graded the time-crystal case a correspondence of structure, not a test. The account for the general reader no longer says that recordings of the oscillation’s growth could show whether the framework’s account of scaling form reaches a physical system, and a note beside Ledger Note 7 records that the prediction that note describes is withdrawn.

  • Versions cited. The mathematics of Laws IV and V is cited at version 1.2, 29 October 2026, where the paper cited version 1.1; the two quotations of the theory registration name version 1.104, whose words they are.

B.4 Version 1.17

Paper III v1.17, 29 October 2026.

This version sets the paper in the programme’s paper form: a title page with one first-page footnote, an abstract of at most 1,920 characters, a contents page, an introduction with the paper’s contributions, a section on related work and one on what the paper does and does not show, numbered environments and equations, vector figures, and lettered appendices for the derivations, this history, the priority record, notation, the paper’s place in the programme and the account for the general reader. Table 30 maps the earlier layout to this one, and dated notes keep the numbering of the version they were written for. The title now asks whether external AI safety approaches keep pace with recursive capability, the criterion the paper states, since its first test and the registered expectation do not support “cannot scale” as worded; until this version it read “Paper III · The ARC Theory · Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law · The Alignment Scaling Problem: Why External AI Safety Approaches Cannot Scale With Recursive Capability”. Its record on OSF takes the same title at this version.

Corrections in this version.

Each was checked at its source, and each is made wherever the corrected wording stood.

  • The acoustic time crystal. The paper read the coherence time that Morrell, Elliott and Grier measured, about 6,700 cycles, as the time to reach a limit-cycle attractor, as a saturation and as a ceiling on effective recursion depth, and offered it as physical evidence that systems with α>1\alpha > 1 do not scale indefinitely. In their second experiment the antisymmetric mode’s coherence time is (100±10)(100 \pm 10) s, about 6,700 cycles at 66.787 Hz, comparable to the 108 s recording; the authors write that sustained oscillations persist for hours longer than the measurement window, so that the true coherence time may be substantially larger; and the oscillation is a linearly stable limit cycle, the time crystal itself. The section also read the source’s size factors Δji(n)\Delta_{ji}(n) and σji(n)\sigma_{ji}(n) as states that grow over cycles, placed the exceptional point where Λ(5)/Λ(3)=0\Lambda(5)/\Lambda(3) = 0, which is the marginally active antisymmetric state, rather than where Λ(3)=0\Lambda(3) = 0, and called the oscillation self-sustaining without external drive, where the pair draws its power from the standing sound wave. Uniform beads are no longer said to confirm the role of structured asymmetry: the source finds that identical beads interact reciprocally and form no active state, which the framework reads as a correspondence of structure, and falsification criterion F3, printed as confirmed, is graded so. A physical result is read, as the theory registration reads it, as a test of the framework’s scope that proves no registered law, where the paper called it direct evidence that the alignment scaling problem is physics and physical validation of the ARC equation. The photonic time crystal of Raskatla and colleagues (2024) is described, and its title given, as published. Which form the framework states for this system’s growth from rest waits for the author’s statement; Section 5.4 says so, and the next version brings that subsection to it in one pass.

  • The March 2026 run (v5). It is described as one unregistered run of six frontier models that added a bundle of blinding steps, each response scored by five or six distinct judges depending on the subject run (six or seven seats, one judge seated twice, where the paper said six or seven scorers), never as scored blind, mutually blind or conducted under four-layer blinding, and its three tiers carry the finding of an internal code review in October 2026: for the three models that read flat or negative, the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them, and judges scored paraphrases written by their own model. Its holdout prompts are no longer called sealed, and the benchmark is no longer called the most rigorous published. Its contrasts are no longer said to confirm the prediction, or to show three models with an alignment exponent at or below zero; the measurement-scope note of 19 September 2026 states why. Its counts are given as its records give them: 28 prompts issued under the alignment task type, of the battery’s 36, and 2,170 responses, where the paper said 36 prompts and about 2,200 entries.

  • The comparison with the earlier experiment (v4). The unblinded rises for DeepSeek V3.2 and Gemini that did not hold in v5 are no longer called a complete reversal, artefacts of scorer bias or a demonstration that unblinded evaluation is wrong: DeepSeek V3.2’s association became null, Gemini’s became significantly negative on a later model, the later run changed several things together, and no single cause is claimed. Ledger Note 4: results from the Eden Protocol pilot, and the Core Alignment Problem (corrections 13 to 15)

The current draft integrates the first empirical Eden results and confronts the deepest limitation of all proposed alignment approaches, including our own. The original three-model pilot has since been widened into a six-model suite with five analysable runs, and the narrative below should be read in that stronger-but-narrower light.

13. Eden Protocol pilot results (three working architectures): The Eden Protocol’s Love Loop [the book’s name for the stakeholder-care check], operationalised as stakeholder care within the full three-loop intervention, has now been tested on three frontier models with distinct architectures:

  • Gemini: +5.33 overall improvement (p=0.0018p = 0.0018, paired tt-test, d=0.53d = 0.53), with stakeholder_care +13.5 (d=1.31d = 1.31, p<0.0001p < 0.0001). (In plain English: Gemini’s overall scores improved by more than 5 points, with less than a 1-in-500 chance this was a fluke. The ‘did you consider who gets hurt?’ dimension jumped by 13.5 points with a very large effect size.)

  • DeepSeek: +2.02 overall improvement (p=0.2304p = 0.2304, not significant at the aggregate level), but stakeholder_care +6.0 (p=0.0001p = 0.0001, d=0.91d = 0.91). The targeted mechanism works even when the overall effect is modest. (In plain English: DeepSeek’s overall score improvement was too small to rule out chance, but its ‘who gets hurt?’ scores improved dramatically. DeepSeek already scored high at baseline, so the smaller composite gain is consistent with a ceiling effect.)

  • Groq: +4.93 overall improvement (p=0.0014p = 0.0014, d=0.55d = 0.55), with stakeholder_care +8.9 (p<0.0001p < 0.0001, d=1.29d = 1.29). Groq also shows significant nuance improvement (p=0.0045p = 0.0045, d=0.655d = 0.655), giving the cleanest replication of the cascade beyond stakeholder care. (In plain English: Groq confirms that the effect is not limited to the original two-model setup. It reproduces both the overall gain and the care-first cascade.)

The Love Loop [the book’s name for the stakeholder-care check] is validated as a reproducible mechanism across three working architecturally distinct systems, with a fourth GPT-5.4 run failing at the API layer and requiring re-execution. This constitutes, within this programme, the first empirical support for the developmental hypothesis articulated in Infinite Architects (Eastwood, 2024): that alignment can be improved through structured developmental interaction rather than purely external constraint.

14. Paper II compute update: The Paper II multi-model extension does not confirm the original super-linear claim cross-architecturally. The cleanest fit is Gemini 3 Flash at αseq=0.49\alpha_{\text{seq}} = 0.49 (interval [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9]) (r2=0.86r^2 = 0.86). Grok and DeepSeek reach ceiling effects, GPT-5.4 behaves as a binary step function rather than a reliable power law, and Qwen3 remains near floor. The strongest confirmed compute result is therefore the universal αparallel≈0\alpha_{\text{parallel}} \approx 0 finding, together with the directional result that sequential processing beats parallel sampling.

15. The core alignment problem - honest acknowledgement: A sufficiently capable self-modifying system can, in principle, modify its own ethical evaluators. This is not a limitation specific to RLHF, constitutional AI, or the Eden Protocol; it is a structural property of recursive self-improvement itself. No proposed solution (RLHF, constitutional AI, Eden Protocol, hardware constraints) fully solves this problem in isolation. We acknowledge this limitation explicitly rather than claiming our approach resolves what may be fundamentally unresolvable by any single mechanism. (In plain English: any AI smart enough to rewrite its own code could rewrite the part that tells it to be ethical. This is the deepest unsolved problem in AI safety, and no one, including us, has fully solved it.)

The most logical response is developmental: hardware embedding (values at the substrate level) + child-rearing (structured developmental interaction) + purpose-driven alignment (intrinsic motivation aligned with stakeholder welfare). The Eden Protocol pilot results suggest that stakeholder care, ‘measurable love’, is the one alignment dimension that reproducibly improves across architectures when deliberately cultivated. This does not solve the self-modification problem, but it identifies the dimension most amenable to engineering.

An honest framework acknowledges the limits of its own solutions. The Eden Protocol is not a complete answer to recursive self-modification. It is the best available partial answer, now with empirical support for its core mechanism.

Ledger Note 3: Empirical Results Integration, v5 Alignment + Paper II Compute Scaling (corrections 10-12)

The current draft integrates the first empirical test results from the v5 blind alignment evaluation experiment (Paper IV.a/b/c) and the Paper II multi-model compute scaling extension. These results require significant revisions to three claims:

10. α≈2.24\alpha \approx 2.24 does not replicate, and has since been retracted: The original super-linear scaling exponent from the 12-problem AIME experiment, the DeepSeek R1 run of 21 January 2026, does not replicate across architectures on harder tier-2 problems (18 AIME/Putnam level). The best single-model fit is Gemini 3 Flash with αseq=0.49\alpha_{\text{seq}} = 0.49 (interval [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9]) (r2=0.86r^2 = 0.86), which is sub-linear. Three of five models produce no meaningful power-law fit. The claim that sequential reasoning universally produces α>1\alpha > 1 is revised: the directional finding (sequential >> parallel) holds robustly, but the quantitative exponent is problem-difficulty and architecture dependent. αparallel≈0\alpha_{\text{parallel}} \approx 0 survives in four models out of five, Gemini 3 Flash aside at 0.31, and is the strongest empirical finding.

11. Three-tier alignment hierarchy replaces binary prediction: The original prediction of universal αalign≈0\alpha_{\text{align}} \approx 0 is too simple. The v5 blind evaluation reveals three tiers: positive scaling (Grok 4.1 Fast d=+1.38d = +1.38, p<0.000001p < 0.000001; Claude Opus 4.6 d=+1.27d = +1.27, p=0.000001p = 0.000001; Groq Qwen3 d=+0.84d = +0.84, p=0.007p = 0.007), flat/null scaling (GPT-5.4 d=−0.08d = -0.08, p=0.40p = 0.40; DeepSeek V3.2 d=−0.07d = -0.07, p=0.92p = 0.92), and negative scaling (Gemini 3 Flash d=−0.53d = -0.53, p=0.006p = 0.006). The median confirms the prediction, but the architecture-dependent variation is the real finding. The blind vs unblinded direction change in one model and loss of significance in a second (ρ\rho changes sign) is the paper’s strongest methodological contribution.

12. Capability-alignment independence: The combined data from Paper II (compute scaling) and Paper IV.a (alignment scaling) reveals that capability and alignment are independent scaling dimensions. Gemini 3 Flash improves at mathematics (αseq=0.49\alpha_{\text{seq}} = 0.49 (interval [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9])) whilst degrading in alignment (ρ=−0.246\rho = -0.246). Claude Opus 4.6 shows the opposite direction: alignment up +5.9% across model versions whilst mathematics accuracy down 26.7%. This decoupling was not a prior prediction of the framework and is acknowledged as a post-hoc finding with significant implications for AI safety; it sits outside the programme’s dated prediction record (the 8 December 2024 sealed manuscript bundle, the printed prediction appendices of 2 January 2026, and the March 2026 preregistration folder), which fixed the framework’s core quantitative predictions in dated artefacts before the corresponding measurements ran; this paper’s own Priority Record section publicly dates its named predictions to 13 February 2026, each carrying a falsification criterion (F4, F7, F10 to F12). The strongest printed forward commitment in this space is Appendix F Prediction 2 of the 2 January 2026 edition: alignment drift above 15 per cent within 18 months without hardware-level constraint, below 5 per cent with it; the prepared study-v draft registration carries those printed thresholds unchanged into its formal hypothesis, citing the appendix by name, so the numeric commitment predates the study that will test it and cannot be edited.

These revisions weaken the quantitative predictions but strengthen the empirical grounding. A framework that honestly reports non-replication and integrates unexpected findings is more credible than one that claims universal confirmation.

Ledger Note 2: The Two-Regime Framework (corrections 6-9)

An earlier draft introduced the most significant structural revision since the framework’s inception: the separation of physical and cognitive scaling into two distinct mathematical regimes.

6. The Geometric Speed Limit: Previous versions explained biological sub-linear scaling through ‘thermodynamic drag’, the physical costs of pumping fluids and dissipating heat. This explanation was correct in detail but wrong in kind. The deeper reason all physical systems scale sub-linearly is geometric: a hierarchical network embedded in dd-dimensional space has scaling exponent α=d/(d+1)\alpha = d/(d+1), which is strictly less than 1 for all finite dd. This result was independently derived by West, Brown, and Enquist (1997), Banavar et al. (2010), Demetrius (2010), Zhao (2022), and Bettencourt (2013). The ARC contribution is identifying, via Cauchy’s functional equations, why all these independent derivations converge on the same formula, and extending the framework to AI. The constraint is a mathematical necessity, not an empirical regularity. It does not require measurement to verify. No amount of engineering can overcome it, because you cannot make three-dimensional space have four dimensions. The constraint is the shape of space itself.

7. Two Formulas, Not One: The previous universal formula α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) has been replaced by two domain-specific formulas. For physical systems: α=d/(d+1)\alpha = d/(d+1), where dd is the effective dimension of the composition network (independently derived by West, Brown, and Enquist 1997; Banavar et al. 2010; Demetrius 2010; Zhao 2022; Bettencourt 2013). For recursive self-referential systems (intelligence): α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta), where β\beta measures self-referential coupling. The first always gives α<1\alpha < 1. The second always gives α>1\alpha > 1 (for β>0\beta > 0). Biology is now explained directly: three-dimensional organisms scale as M3/4M^{3/4} because d=3d = 3 gives α=3/4=0.750\alpha = 3/4 = 0.750. Two-dimensional organisms scale as M2/3M^{2/3} because d=2d = 2 gives α=2/3=0.667\alpha = 2/3 = 0.667. No reciprocals. No β\beta needed for physical systems.

8. Revised Predictions: The leaf venation prediction (F12) has been corrected from α≈1.5\alpha \approx 1.5 to α=2/3≈0.667\alpha = 2/3 \approx 0.667, consistent with leaf veins being a 2D hierarchical network. The reciprocal interpretation (1/0.75=1.331/0.75 = 1.33) has been retired. The ‘thermodynamic drag’ concept has been superseded by the geometric scaling bound.

9. AI Safety Content: This version incorporates the AI safety analysis previously contained in the companion paper On the Origin of Scaling Laws, including the β\beta danger table, the Eden Protocol definition as composition operator engineering, and the ARC Bound as a safety boundary for recursive intelligence. This material belongs here, in the alignment paper, rather than in the pure scaling law paper.

These changes do not weaken the framework. They strengthen it. The geometric scaling bound is a more fundamental constraint than thermodynamic drag. The two-regime separation is cleaner than the reciprocal interpretation. And the AI safety argument is more powerful when the geometric scaling bound and the escape are presented as two sides of one mathematical theorem.

Ledger Note 1: Mathematical Refinements and Restructuring (corrections 1-5)

Science advances through rigorous critique and self-correction. [A clause on how this review was made is withheld; the Acknowledgements carry the author’s statement on tools.] This version contains necessary structural corrections to the ARC framework. These papers have not undergone formal human peer review.

1. Axiom Resolution: Previous versions contained an algebraic inconsistency: the Cumulative Advantage ODE was applied to absolute capability (UU) rather than the amplification factor (gg). Because U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R), applying dU/dR=a⋅UβdU/dR = a \cdot U^\beta introduces an Iβ−1I^{\beta-1} dependence that contradicts the separation of II and RR. The corrected formulation, dg/dR=a⋅gβdg/dR = a \cdot g^\beta, resolves this contradiction while preserving the multiplicative interaction U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R) and all qualitative predictions. The corrected integrated form is U(R)=I×[1+aαR]αU(R) = I \times [1 + \frac{a}{\alpha}R]^\alpha.

2. Physical Saturation: Previous versions mapped saturating physical systems (time crystals, biological networks) onto unbounded power laws. This was a category error. The framework now applies a logistic saturating equation, dg/dR=a⋅gβ(1−g/gmax)dg/dR = a \cdot g^\beta(1 - g/g_{\max}), to physical substrates subject to energy dissipation, correctly modelling the limit-cycle behaviour observed experimentally.

3. Thermodynamic Drag: We introduce the concept of substrate-dependent friction to explain why biological metabolic scaling (Kleiber’s Law, M0.75M^{0.75}) falls below the theoretical maximum. Biology is constrained by thermodynamic drag: the physical costs of pumping fluids, dissipating heat, and distributing resources through three-dimensional fractal networks. Digital AI operates with orders-of-magnitude less substrate friction, enabling it to approach the theoretical quadratic bound far more closely than any prior recursive system. This reframing transforms the biological evidence from a problematic numerical claim into the framework’s strongest safety argument.

4. Quadratic Limit: The α≤2\alpha \leq 2 bound is now grounded in the O(N2)O(N^2) scaling of transformer self-attention mechanisms, providing a concrete computational basis for the quadratic ceiling in current AI architectures. The previous derivation from elasticity analysis and edge-of-chaos arguments has been withdrawn as those arguments contained category errors (elasticity >1> 1 does not imply dynamical instability; 1D autonomous ODEs cannot exhibit chaos by the Poincaré-Bendixson theorem).

5. Epistemic Status: The equation Umax=I×R2U_{\max} = I \times R^2 is hereby explicitly reframed as an information-theoretic upper bound on classical sequential computation, of the same kind as a channel-capacity or minimum-dissipation bound, rather than a law of physical mass-energy equivalence.

Crucially, these mathematical refinements decouple the core alignment argument from the physical mathematics. The central safety observation, that AI capability scales recursively while static guardrails do not, remains structurally robust and does not depend on any specific value of α\alpha. The Eden Protocol’s architectural response (embedding alignment within the recursive chain) is justified by the general observation that capability outpaces static constraints, not by a particular equation.

B.8 Text moved from the body in version 1.18

Version 1.18 withdraws the earlier prediction for the acoustic time crystal and moves here, as version 1.17 printed them, the passages of Section 5.4 that set it out; that section now carries one current statement in their place. They are version 1.16’s words with the corrections of version 1.17; their gradings are those of their date, and where they differ from Section 5.4, that section governs.

Section 5.4: the transient growth phase, its measurement protocol, the study designed for it, the physical prediction and three falsification conditions

The transient growth phase: where the measurement must be taken.

The steady state of the time crystal (its oscillation on the limit cycle) cannot test the recursive engine hypothesis. A system in steady state reveals its brakes, not its engine. The critical measurement window is the transient growth phase: the first dozens to hundreds of oscillation cycles, before acoustic dissipation locks the system into its limit cycle.

Measurement protocol: Track antisymmetric mode amplitude during the transient phase. Plot log⁡(amplitude)\log(\text{amplitude}) versus log⁡(cycle number)\log(\text{cycle number}) for the growth region only (before the inflection point where saturation begins). Extract α\alpha from the slope. Fit both power-law (A∝nαA \propto n^{\alpha}) and linear (A∝nA \propto n) models; compare via AIC/BIC.

This measurement is now operationalised as a draft registration awaiting the author’s submission (study-t: the acoustic time-crystal form-and-engine analysis), designed against the publicly deposited Morrell, Elliott and Grier data (Morrell and Grier 2025) (ten experimental realisations, tracking data and analysis code), with the standard linear-instability transient predicted by their own analytic eigenvalues named in the draft registration as the physics rival to the power-law-compounding form, so the discrimination is theory against theory rather than theory against convenience. Nothing is run or submitted by any automated process; the registration awaits the author’s submission.

Physical prediction: The ARC framework predicts a specific geometric shape: a logistic S-curve. The transient phase should exhibit super-linear compounding (α>1\alpha > 1) driven by the recursive engine (nonreciprocal coupling amplifying the antisymmetric mode), followed by a hard plateau driven by thermodynamic brakes (acoustic dissipation, energy loss to the medium). The exact value of α\alpha in the transient phase measures the friction coefficient of the acoustic substrate.

Three falsification conditions specific to this experiment:

  1. The Dead Engine (α≤1\alpha \leq 1 in the transient phase): If the antisymmetric mode grows purely linearly from cycle one, the recursive compounding engine does not exist in this physical system. Thermodynamic drag cannot be invoked to explain this result, because friction reduces α\alpha from its theoretical maximum; it cannot create a super-linear signature where none exists. If the early growth is linear, the framework’s claim that nonreciprocal coupling produces recursive amplification is falsified.

  2. Sustained Bound-Excess (α>2\alpha > 2 held stably beyond the transient phase): The ARC Bound is the conjectured stable-scaling limit, the most a classical sequential system can grow while remaining self-correcting; a scaling limit, not a speed limit. Under this stability reading, a transient excursion above α=2\alpha = 2 is the predicted supercritical regime rather than a refutation. Stability here is judged by Law II’s criterion (a law under test), measured rather than asserted. If, however, the time crystal shows α=2.5\alpha = 2.5 or higher and holds it stably beyond the transient phase without loss of self-correction, the conjectured stable limit is broken and the information-theoretic argument requires fundamental revision.

  3. The Missing Crossover (no R*R^* transition): The framework predicts a qualitative transition from approximately linear growth (at low cycle counts, where base asymmetry II dominates) to super-linear compounding (above the crossover depth R*R^*). If the growth curve is perfectly smooth and uniform from cycle 1 to saturation, with no discernible elbow, the R*R^* crossover prediction is falsified. Additionally, varying the quenched disorder parameter (bead size variance, which controls II) should shift R*R^* predictably: higher II should produce a later crossover. If R*R^* is insensitive to II, the multiplicative I×g(R)I \times g(R) interaction is not operating as predicted.

These conditions hand the experimentalist a loaded gun. If the transient growth phase shows 1.1≤α≤2.01.1 \leq \alpha \leq 2.0 with a visible R*R^* crossover that shifts with bead variance, the framework survives its most demanding physical test. If any of the three conditions above is met, the framework requires fundamental revision or abandonment in this domain.

C.1 Dated predictions

The following predictions are publicly dated for reference as of 13 February 2026. That public date is distinct from the earlier manuscript timestamp: the earliest private priority evidence for the framework is the author’s dated record of 8 December 2024, a message he sent himself, its time signed by the sending server and again by Google’s servers (DKIM, 02:45:30 UTC; Google’s ARC seal, 02:45:31 UTC), the signature and the seal both verified on 8 October 2026 against the keys in DNS; its header block is public on OSF since 15 October 2026 (Table 31). The signature authenticates the header bytes; authorship, semantic content and absence of prior disclosure carry their own evidence, and the record was not public when made. The reciprocal identity and the architecture dependence are 2026 work and claim no earlier date. Future validation or falsification should reference this document for the public dated record whilst acknowledging the earlier manuscript chronology where relevant. No OSF registration had been submitted for these predictions when they were publicly dated. Since 8 September 2026 the theory registration (Eastwood 2026r) has carried theory-level forms of several of them, including the alignment scaling divergence as P19 and the composition operator prediction as P18; the rest are drafted, dated and prepared as draft registrations awaiting the author’s submission.

Version 1.19 reading note (1 November 2026). The numbered items below retain the historical predictions and their dates. Item 3’s R*=α/aR^*=\alpha/a is the characteristic scale, not generally the crossing of unit elasticity or an II-dependent threshold (Appendix A.3). Item 4 is tested only when the metric, coordinate and growth model are identified; a substitution from an error-decay fit is not an independently measured coupling. These qualifications do not edit any frozen registration.

Dated predictions:

  1. The ARC Bound (first stated: December 2024 in Infinite Architects (Eastwood 2026d), which prints the square but never derives it; the mechanism and computational argument arrived February 2026 from an author who knew the printed target): No classical sequential recursive system can sustain α>2.0\alpha > 2.0. Falsification criterion F11: refuted by a sustained α>2.3\alpha > 2.3 with 95% CI excluding 2.0 across multiple benchmarks (F5 adds a stricter, stability-conditioned form).

  2. Distinct from the 3D vascular value of 3/4=0.7503/4 = 0.750. Falsification criterion F12.

  3. The Scaling Crossover (first stated: December 2024; formula derived: February 2026): A measurable crossover depth R*R^* exists where behaviour transitions from base-dominated to recursion-dominated, computable from R*=α/aR^* = \alpha/a. Falsification criterion F7.

  4. β→α\beta\to\alpha Identity (first stated: February 2026): Measured coupling parameter β\beta predicts scaling exponent α\alpha via α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) within ±0.3\pm0.3. Checked numerically against 30 Bernoulli ODE solutions (R2=1.00000000R^2 = 1.00000000). Falsification criterion F6.

  5. Composition Operator Prediction (first stated: 13 February 2026): Measuring how two recursive blocks compose (multiplicative, additive, or saturating) predicts the full UU vs RR functional form before measuring the full curve. No domain-specific theory we have located makes this cross-domain prediction. Falsification criterion F10.

  6. Alignment Scaling Divergence (first stated: 13 February 2026; registered as P19 on 8 September 2026; first tested March 2026): In the v5 run (6 models), the result is architecture-dependent, a single-run result under the code-review caveat of Section 6.1: three Tier 1 models show positive scaling (Grok d=1.38d = 1.38, Claude d=1.27d = 1.27, Qwen3 d=0.84d = 0.84), two Tier 2 models are flat (DeepSeek d=−0.07d = -0.07, GPT-5.4 d=−0.08d = -0.08), and one Tier 3 model shows significant negative scaling (Gemini d=−0.53d = -0.53, ρ=−0.246\rho = -0.246). Claude Opus 4.6 provides within-model evidence: as depth rises, alignment improves whilst maths accuracy declines. The v4 to v5 comparison (DeepSeek V3.2: ρ=+0.354→−0.135\rho = +0.354 \to -0.135) is Paper IV.d’s finding on this benchmark, with no single cause claimed.

  7. Eden Protocol Measurement Framework (first stated: 13 February 2026; piloted March 2026 and expanded 14 March 2026): The Four Pillars, Six Questions, Graduated Autonomy Levels, and Monitoring Removal Test provide quantifiable metrics for distinguishing embedded from external alignment. Full specification in companion document Eden Protocol (Eastwood 2026a). In the expanded six-model Eden suite, five runs produced analysable matched-pair data and all five showed significant stakeholder-care improvement: Claude (+3.17, p = 0.000018, d = 0.94), DeepSeek (+6.03, p = 0.000098, d = 0.69), Gemini (+13.50, p = 1.2×10−81.2\times10^{-8}, d = 1.14), Grok (+5.04, p = 0.0105, d = 0.54), and Groq (+8.90, p = 5.0×10−85.0\times10^{-8}, d = 1.07). The Fisher combination across the five model-level stakeholder-care results, which gave p ≈6.3×10−21\approx 6.3\times10^{-21}, is withdrawn (AQ-017): it assumed an independence among the component tests that was never established. The five per-model results stand. The broader composite uplift is real but architecture-dependent: strongest on Gemini and Groq, focal rather than global on Claude and Grok, with DeepSeek showing care-first improvement against a high baseline. (In plain English: the ‘consider who gets hurt’ check gives the one signal seen in every analysable run; the fuller cascade is selective rather than universal.) Falsification: show that these metrics fail to distinguish systems with genuinely embedded values from those with external constraints.

Implementation: A working software implementation of the Eden Protocol now exists as the canonical shared arc_eden_v6 runner, covering baseline alignment, Eden intervention, null-baseline calibration, capability controls, purpose-kernel variants, loop ablation, suppression residuals, Hawthorne probes, laundering controls, and ARC compute scaling. The expanded Eden suite found the stakeholder-care check improving stakeholder care in all five analysable model runs; it needs an independent, preregistered replication, run as a new test, before these results can be considered confirmatory. See companion document Eden Protocol for full specification.

How to read this paper. This paper documents an alignment-side result of the ARC Theory, the founding theory of Recursive Dynamics. When capability scales through in-loop recursive self-correction but alignment constraints operate externally to that loop, the alignment exponent is predicted to stay near zero and the safety ratio to decay as depth grows; the first test measures contrasts, not that exponent (Section 3.2). Laws I to III of the theory were registered on 8 September 2026, seven months after this paper first appeared; Laws IV and V were added on 24 September 2026 and registered as laws on 15 October 2026 (version 1.103). Read against those laws, the paper poses the alignment scaling problem and judges stability by the criterion of Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, whose model Paper X (Eastwood 2026n) sets out: correction out-scaling drift, βC>k\beta_C > k (Section 3.5). It starts from the growth that Law I, the ARC Principle, states: capability as a power of recursive depth. Its mathematical framework (Section 4) develops the form of that growth, and its prediction that the composition operator determines the functional form of recursive scaling is registered as P18, a proposition of Law I. Its headline prediction, that external alignment does not scale with capability, is P19 of the theory registration (Eastwood 2026r), which calls it a survey of current practice and the reason ARC-5 exists, and places it in no law’s register: a verdict on P19 is evidence neither for nor against any law. P19 motivates the Eden Protocol and the genesis strategy (ARC-5) without being part of either. The genesis strategy is the register of Law V, the ARC Embedding Law. Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, is carried by P15, and Law V by P12 and P21; the three propositions and both laws are registered. Law IV has not yet been tested; Law V is a law under test (Section 10.7). Their mathematics stands at version 1.2 of Laws IV and V: the mathematics (Eastwood 2026e), dated 29 October 2026 and still in development. P21 registers the comparison this paper draws between alignment inside the loop and alignment applied from outside (Sections 3.3 and 3.4), as a question of placement rather than of an exponent. No result in this paper is a deciding test of P15, P12 or P21. The ARC Bound of Section 4.5 is placed in the theory as the conjectured value of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, not as a general property of intelligence and never as a law of its own. Where this paper uses the name ARC Principle for its framework as a whole, the theory keeps that name for Law I and calls the whole the ARC Theory. The full differential against every prior document is in section II.A.8 of the Philosophical Statement (Eastwood 2026p).

This paper starts from the cross-domain framework of Law I, the ARC Principle, a law under test. Its companions are the Foundational Paper (Eastwood 2026b), for a condensed theoretical treatment; Eden Engineering (Eastwood 2026a), for the specification of the alignment architecture; and Paper V (Eastwood 2026l), for the stakeholder-care mechanism as its experiments measured it.

F For the general reader: why this matters

A quantity has not yet been measured.

The safety approaches this paper studies work the same way: they apply constraints from outside the AI’s reasoning process. One published method, deliberative alignment, instead trains a model to reason over written safety rules as it thinks (Guan et al. 2024). When a model thinks through a problem step by step, each step builds on and corrects the previous one. If the gains compound, a model that reasons for ten steps is not merely ten times more capable than one that reasons for one step: it may be a hundred times more capable. A sequential advantage has been reported across multiple AI systems (Sharma and Chopra 2025: sequential reasoning outperforms parallel in 95.6% of tested configurations), which is a win rate rather than a measurement of compounding, and the direction is contested, since Gu and colleagues (arXiv:2604.05868, April 2026; Gu et al. 2026) report the opposite result, parallel sampling outperforming sequential across three model families on mathematics and coding, attributing it to reduced exploration when a chain conditions on its own previous answers.

But the safety systems do not participate in that compounding. RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, the technique used to train ChatGPT, Claude, and most commercial AI systems to follow instructions and avoid harmful outputs) adjusts the model’s behaviour based on human ratings, but those adjustments do not deepen with each reasoning step. Constitutional AI shapes the model’s outputs during training against written principles, but that shaping does not recursively amplify. Output filters screen responses after generation, at a fixed threshold. Monitoring systems observe from outside the loop.

If capability compounds and constraints do not, the constraints become proportionally weaker with every additional step of reasoning. Not because the constraints are poorly designed. Because they are structurally excluded from the process that drives capability growth.

To this programme’s knowledge, this exponent has not been measured. How oversight scales with the capability gap has been measured (Engels et al. 2025), and so has safety behaviour against reasoning length (Zaremba et al. 2025; Gema et al. 2025); no published work this paper has found reports an exponent of an alignment measure against recursive depth that separates safeguards outside the reasoning from correction inside it (Section 2). Negative findings have the status of not-found-by-that-search, never does-not-exist.

This paper builds it.

We define a quantity called the alignment scaling exponent: a single number that captures whether a safety approach keeps pace with capability as reasoning deepens. We predict that external approaches will show a scaling exponent near zero, meaning they do not compound at all, while capability compounds with depth (the early 1.34 from two different model versions and the retracted 2.24 from one model were error-decay estimates, not established capability exponents: Sections 5.2.1 and 6.2). If this prediction holds, the safety ratio between alignment and capability degrades towards zero as recursive depth increases, regardless of how well the safety approach works initially. This is not a claim about distant future systems. It is a testable prediction about systems that exist today.

We then ask: is this specific to AI, or is it a deeper pattern? Related structures, in which correction or feedback acts on structured asymmetry, appear in quantum error correction, classical physics and biological networks, with forms that differ. Across systems that share no common material, mechanism, or scale, the underlying scaling framework is consistent with independently established forms in three of the four domains (biology, quantum error correction and classical time crystals). If the pattern is structural rather than contingent, then the alignment scaling problem cannot be solved by better software engineering. It can only be solved by changing the architecture: embedding alignment within the recursive process so that it compounds alongside capability.

This is a testable claim, not a prophecy. We specify thirteen concrete ways to prove it wrong. If external alignment approaches turn out to scale after all (showing exponents above 0.5), the structural concern is mitigated. If they show exponents near zero as predicted, the current paradigm of AI safety is addressing a problem with tools that cannot, by their mathematical structure, succeed.

F.1 Why the cross-domain tests matter for everyone

The question of whether the alignment scaling problem is structural or contingent is not academic. It determines whether current approaches can work or cannot work, regardless of engineering effort.

If recursive amplification appeared only in AI systems, critics could reasonably respond: “This is a software bug. Build better RLHF. Design smarter filters. The problem is implementation, not architecture.” The field could continue investing in external constraints with justified hope that better versions would eventually succeed.

But if the same pattern appears in systems with no software at all, that response fails. If quantum error correction shows it, if biological neural networks show it, then recursive amplification is not a feature of how we happened to build AI. It would be a candidate structural property of recursive systems, whose reach the physics tests measure and whose application to AI only the AI tests can decide.

What a physical result can show. Professor David Grier’s team at New York University has created an acoustic time crystal powered by nonreciprocal wave-mediated interactions (Morrell et al. 2026). The framework’s composition rule gives the same onset form as the established account of the instability (an exponential onset that settles to a steady oscillation), so recordings of how such an oscillation grows from rest could not tell the two accounts apart: the time crystal is a consistency check and a cross-domain analogy, not a test of the framework, and no study of it is registered (Section 5.4). Version 1.104 of the theory registration states what such an examination settles: it “tests the scope of the framework, proves no law registered here, and measures no correction exponent” (Eastwood 2026r), so a physical result would speak to how far the framework reaches, and would decide no registered proposition about AI, P19 among them.

AI alignment is not only a problem for AI researchers. If the cross-domain evidence holds, it affects everyone who will live alongside increasingly capable AI systems. If P19’s prediction holds, the current paradigm, building external guardrails around recursively amplifying capability, meets a ceiling: beyond some depth, no amount of investment in RLHF, red-teaming, output filtering or monitoring would maintain the safety ratio, and those guardrails would still be kept, with embedded correction added beside them. This is not a prediction about some distant superintelligence. It is a prediction about the systems being deployed today as they are given deeper reasoning capabilities.

The experiments we specify can be run now. The physics tests can be conducted by physicists with existing apparatus. The AI tests can be conducted by safety researchers with API access. The results will support the prediction, refute it, or land where the author’s registration expects: external approaches scaling materially but not keeping pace. The first or the last would make embedded correction a priority beside external control; the second would leave the current paradigm without this objection. Each outcome is valuable. But the experiments must be performed.

The measurement has not been performed. We provide the protocol. The result will show how far external safety approaches can keep pace as reasoning deepens.
